title: Explaining the stock market: Why is it still so hard?
author: Bryan Kelly, Yinan Su, Chao Zhang
description: Physicists could already explain the motion of planets with extraordinary precision centuries ago. Finance still struggles to explain yesterday’s stock market movement. This column identifies a foundational failure of empirical asset pricing and makes significant progress towards explaining market movements using AI. title: The demographics of technology adoption and productivity growth
author: Nils H. Lehr
description: Advanced economies are counting on artificial intelligence to revive productivity growth just as their workforces age. This column argues that the two trends are closely connected, because young workers adopt new technologies at far higher rates than old workers. Evidence from US local labour markets shows that younger workforces adopt more technology, see faster wage growth, and generate more innovation. A model calibrated to these responses attributes about one quarter of the late-1990s US productivity boom to the baby boom’s youth wave. Workforce ageing is thus a headwind to adoption-driven growth, though it need not diminish the gains from an AI-scale breakthrough.

title: High spending, low impact: Can Germany’s defence policy deliver on strategic ambition – and deter Russia?
author: jon.wallace
description:
High spending, low impact: Can Germany’s defence policy deliver on strategic ambition – and deter Russia? Expert comment jon.wallace 25 November 2026

An unpopular government must train its civil service how to deliver a strategy at a time of technological upheaval – while persuading a sceptical public. It has some resources to draw on.

The significant increase in German defence spending since 2022 has been celebrated as a success story for European security. Germany has the stated ambition to become the largest land power in Europe, with a core defence budget set to rise to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2029.

To support this effort, some initial procurement reforms are already taking place: plans were unveiled earlier in the year to reform the defence procurement agency. But Germany still struggles with the strategic and cultural transformation across society that will be necessary to realize its ambitions.

In its political and military leadership, there is an incomplete understanding of how German deterrence is meant to work, what kind of a future conflict to expect and as a result, what systems Germany needs to acquire. That risks making the increased defence spending inefficient, undermining fragile public support for rearmament. And it could send confusing signals to industry.

The challenge is complex. And it comes at a time of technological, political and strategic upheaval. But Germany has important resources to draw on.

A clear strategy

Like many NATO allies, Germany has updated its security and defence strategic documents over the last few years. At first glance, these look comparable to those of other NATO nations. But Germany continues to struggle to translate them into action.

Part of this challenge might be that some documents, such as the Bundeswehr’s military strategy published in 2026, were produced for the first time. Other NATO countries have established pathways for turning a strategy into action, but Germany has to figure it out from scratch.

What’s more, in some cases procurement has come ahead of the strategy. That partly makes sense: Germany could not wait until 2026 to start acquiring new systems, considering the changed security environment. But it also seems to have inhibited procurement reform, sent mixed messages to industry and led to some disjointed and traditional contracts. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Examples of this include post-contract adjustments to a large order of Boxer armoured vehicles. Additionally, traditional procurement types have been prioritized to date: orders placed have tended towards big, traditional equipment – frigates, helicopters, armoured vehicles.

These are all important and the Bundeswehr needs more of them. However, in the NATO comparison, the Bundeswehr compares poorly for orders placed for uncrewed systems and digital support infrastructure.

Meanwhile, Berlin is struggling to adapt to the pace of technological change in war, and its effect on deterrence. Newer military technologies complicate old assumptions about the balance between conventional and nuclear deterrence. Some advanced conventional capabilities, such as deep precision strike, are taking on parts of a traditionally nuclear deterrence mission.

But NATO thinking since the end of the cold war created silos where nuclear and conventional capabilities were seen as entirely separate, rather than as levers of the same concept of deterrence. This means that non-nuclear allies like Germany have not invested much thought in how their militaries can deter. Conventional militaries’ role was traditionally to defend, not deter aggression or fight to win. The absence of good understanding of what to deter and what kind of fight to expect hampers German decision making when it comes to military procurement.

Germany now needs to find a way to upskill its officials and civil servants to better understand deterrence concepts, especially how to tailor deterrence according to the perceptions of its potential adversaries.

These discussions must be had across a broad spectrum of the German political and military leadership. There needs to be a consensus understanding of what Russia has learned from the war in Ukraine, how it is applying these lessons to its thinking about war with NATO, and what capability gaps Germany and other NATO countries have.

Public opinion

Germany’s security leadership also faces a domestic challenge. The German government has struggled to take the public along with its messaging on the re-armament agenda and especially support for Ukraine.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz won election on a platform that included stronger support for Ukraine. But his handling of domestic issues has seen his popularity plunge to the lowest on record for a German chancellor.

Falling support for the government is mirrored by the rise of the far-right party Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). A significant majority of its supporters oppose support for Ukraine, and its leadership does not see Russia as a threat to Germany. It would likely be a serious challenge to EU and NATO cooperation on European security were the AfD to become a party of government.

Mending fences

An additional political factor Germany has to navigate is how to define its new European security leadership role in relation to its neighbours.

Allies like Poland remain uncomfortable with the idea of Germany providing security leadership for Europe. That is especially true in the context of rising AfD support. ‘We remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,’ said Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski in September, following the AfD’s record result in the regional Saxony-Anhalt election. 

Germany and Poland will both be part of the negotiations for upcoming Ukraine peace talks. Polish negotiators will undoubtedly watch very carefully for any signs of German concessions towards Russia, as Poland has long been critical of the former German approach of prioritizing business relations with Russia.

These factors combine for a difficult burden: Germany needs to navigate internal cultural and structural reform as well as a difficult domestic landscape, while being under the scrutiny of its allies.

The way forward

Germany does have resources it can draw on. When seeking to upskill its officials in deterrence doctrine, it can learn from NATO partners’ plans: the UK also recognized it has lost deterrence knowledge across its civil service and is running regular training courses for civil servants. Germany also has a vibrant academic community specializing in strategic thinking – people who would welcome working more closely with government and delivering some of this work.

Procurement reform has been written about widely, but a simple and affordable improvement might be for the German government to be more disciplined in publishing a list of priorities for procurement, so that industry can react and compete accordingly.

Perhaps more challenging is how to better engage Germany’s neighbours. The German government has tried a range of different confidence-building measures with Poland, similar to its efforts that helped transform the relationship with France. 

However, Polish concerns about Russia and its suspicion of Germany run deep. It will take time to strengthen those relationships. Germany will also have to demonstrate that the ‘Zeitenwende’ is a real, long-term, sustained change, maintaining its current focus on security and defence. Its leading role in the NATO forward deployment, and participation in joint Baltic and Eastern flank exercises will play a significant role here.

In order to bring its people along, the German government needs to develop a sustained and coherent narrative about the risk the country faces from Russia, and all that it is doing to keep Germany safe, and German democracy strong and free. 

It will also need to improve its messaging especially for young Germans. It must highlight the opportunities it is creating for them, rather than scaring them with mixed messages on forced conscription – when they are already dissatisfied with their employment and educational opportunities.

title: Europe still isn’t ready for grey zone warfare
author: thilton.drupal
description:
Europe still isn’t ready for grey zone warfare Expert comment thilton.drupal 24 November 2026

As Russia and Iran intensify their grey zone attacks across the UK and Europe, national governments must improve their defences. They should begin by improving how they identify the perpetrators and communicate the dangers to the public.

Spoiled food and fires in France, a botched drone attack at Leipzig Airport in Germany and flights grounded by bomb threats in the UK and across the continent are only some of the recent grey zone attacks to hit Europe. 

As Europe’s adversaries – primarily Russia and Iran – increase the intensity and frequency of their grey zone attacks, national governments have been cautious and disjointed in their response. Governments need a stronger, collective response to avoid dangerous escalation.

Not quite war, not quite peace

The UK Ministry of Defence defines grey zone, or ‘sub-threshold,’ attacks as those which do not usually meet the legal definition of an act of war. Election interference, disinformation campaigns, cyberattacks, sabotage, harassment from drones, and manufactured security hoaxes all fall within this category.

Recently, Russia and Iran have presented the most significant state-based grey zone threats to Europe. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, European states have fallen victim to an increasing number of grey zone attacks from Russia. Iran significantly intensified its grey zone efforts in Europe after the US and Israel launched strikes against it in late February 2026. China and North Korea, in addition to non-state actors like cybercrime syndicates, have also been previously accused of engaging in grey zone tactics across Europe.

Related work

The resilience gap: Are Europe’s societies ready for the next crisis?

The appeal of grey zone warfare lies in the ability of perpetrators to sow confusion and disunity among targeted populations and trigger failure in critical infrastructure systems, with the aim of gaining a strategic advantage without having to engage in full-blown armed conflict. Myriad grey zone attacks can strain governments’ resources, divide public opinion and distract attention. Internationally, they can also weaken cooperation towards shared objectives. 

European governments see Russia’s grey zone attacks as aimed at hampering their support and assistance for Ukraine. Russia is also likely testing European NATO allies’ capacity to absorb grey zone aggression without triggering its Article 5 mutual defence provisions. Tehran likely aims to disincentivise Europe from aligning with US and Israeli foreign policy objectives in the Middle East and is less likely than Russia to intend these attacks to be the instigation of outright conflict. 

Treading too lightly

To date, European national governments have struggled to effectively respond to grey zone activity in a way that deters future attacks. 

The nature of grey zone tactics inherently complicates the ability of European governments to respond or retaliate. They usually fall short of explicit acts of war, are difficult to immediately attribute to perpetrators, and mimic natural disruptions. 

European governments do not want grey zone attacks to lead to outright direct war with Russia or Iran, but this does not mean that they are not responding to these attacks. 

For example, Estonia has already publicly initiated court proceedings against Russian saboteurs who allegedly attempted to commit arson against a UAV manufacturer on 14 November. France has named Iran’s Revolutionary Guards as responsible for the October 2026 supermarket refrigerator hacks.

Germany, too, was quick to identify Russia for conducting the failed Leipzig Airport bomb attack in August 2026, acknowledging in a statement that the attack was part of ‘hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine’. In the same statement, the government affirmed the likelihood of similar attacks in the future while insisting that Germany is ‘not at war.’ Similarly, the commander of the UK’s Cyber and Specialist Operations Command recently stated that the UK is not ‘at war, but we’re not at peace either.’ 

European countries have responded to attacks by seemingly accepting that they will be a constant target of grey zone warfare, but they have generally failed to translate these warnings into a wider public awareness of the escalatory potential of these attacks. 

Attribution of recent attacks is helpful in establishing blame, but without wider public awareness of Russian, Iranian, and other sustained grey zone campaigns across the continent, there is a risk that the public misunderstands these attacks as one-off incidents. 

Europe should acknowledge that it is effectively under coordinated attack and communicate this publicly. Without securing public support for strengthened resilience measures, especially around critical infrastructure, Europe will remain limited to responses that are clandestine, reactive, and disjointed. 

Protecting infrastructure

The UK and other European governments must find ways to enhance security measures around critical infrastructure, given the increasing frequency with which it is being targeted. To respond more effectively, governments first need to take more preventive steps to protect their most obvious vulnerabilities to grey zone attacks.

Poland’s army, for example, was tasked in December 2025 to protect key energy infrastructure. Shortly after the freezer hacks in Europe, the UK’s proactive identification of a cybersecurity flaw enabled a cross-sector awareness campaign that prevented a similar hack occurring. 

Related work

After the RAF Fairford incident, the UK should develop its homeland defence forces

These kinds of measures signal a deeper readiness within national governments to deter grey zone attacks, though they are not without their costs: for example, dedicating military forces to protect infrastructure could impede frontline readiness. 

It is also harder for Western European countries to secure the domestic political will required for proactive defence than countries in Eastern Europe that are closer to Russia. In Western Europe, governments are less likely to feel confident to take drastic measures that could be interpreted domestically as initiating unnecessary conflict or increasing defence spending amid rising concerns over the cost of living. In September 2026, for example, only 40 per cent of British residents surveyed by YouGov thought Russia posed a major threat to Europe beyond Ukraine.

Garnering political will

Western European governments therefore need to generate political will for improved defence against grey zone warfare. As a first step towards this, governments must invest in the creation and dissemination of awareness campaigns and resources mapping the comprehensive nature of attacks from Russia, Iran, and other malign actors. 

This information needs to be disseminated by verifiable and credible outlets and departments, in anticipation of disinformation already being a demonstrated grey zone tactic. Awareness efforts also must go beyond individual attack attribution and explicitly connect various separate attacks, both domestically and transnationally. Clear messaging enables the public to understand the greater threat posed by grey zone attacks. Governments could also draw upon existing civil society efforts to map grey zone attacks, such as the Ukrainian think-tank Sahaidachnyi Security Center’s sub-threshold warfare tracker, to illustrate the threat to the public. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Increasing public awareness of what is at stake from further grey zone attacks might help persuade the public to support greater defensive measures, including an increase in defence spending to address grey zone vulnerabilities. 

This would help governments to make the case for a two-pronged approach of supplying aid to Ukraine while investing in infrastructure security tailored to specific national and regional needs. Financially, this might also be less expensive overall than exclusively focusing on rearming national militaries for a future conflict.

Without a more forward-looking and unified approach to grey zone attacks, Europe runs the very real risk of offering Russia, Iran and other aggressors the upper hand in any future conflict escalation scenario. The risks of inaction far outweigh any costs of acting now.

description: This report responds to the request of the Ministry of Finance (MOF) of Georgia and has benefited from strong collaboration also with Ministry of Environmental Protection and Agriculture (MEPA) and Rural Development Agency in Georgia. Section 1 introduces the report, providing contextual background and a brief overview of agricultural performance. Section 2 summarizes the technical findings from the public expenditure review of Georgia’s agriculture sector, including an analysis of policy coherence. title: Europe should fund Ukraine’s defence industry as a partner, not a supplier
author: jon.wallace
description:
Europe should fund Ukraine’s defence industry as a partner, not a supplier Expert comment jon.wallace 23 November 2026

Ukraine’s strikes on the Kerch Bridge and Russian navy show the extent of its defence industry’s abilities. The EU 2027 finance package should seek to boost that industry towards a lasting partnership.

In mid-November, Ukrainian forces destroyed a road span of the Kerch Bridge, linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia. The strike used jet-powered drones and cruise missiles reportedly guided through an airborne relay network rather than Starlink. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the bridge strike as the seventh phase of an operation that had first targeted the air-defence, radar and electronic warfare systems protecting the crossing. 

Sequencing of that kind, combining several weapon types using communications under Ukrainian control, owes much to Ukrainian military planning. But the weapons and the relay network themselves reflect a Ukrainian defence sector that has learned to design, field and adapt systems in months, rather than the years typical of European procurement. 
The strike package was not wholly Ukrainian: Destinus, a Dutch-headquartered company, says its systems were the only foreign-made weapons used. Russia’s embassy in The Hague responded by asking publicly whether the Netherlands had joined the war. 

Days later, on 22 November, Kyiv said seven Ukrainian-made sea drones had successfully sunk the Russian corvette Merkury at the Benghazi Naval base in Libya. Unlike Kerch, this attack appears to have involved no foreign weapons, showing the kind of low-cost maritime capability Ukraine has developed and can exercise at range.

Ukraine’s innovation advantage

Ukraine’s defence industry has developed under conditions that no European procurement system faces. Weapons and systems are tested in an active warzone, providing immediate operational feedback and demanding compressed procurement cycles. Its production capacity has grown from around $1 billion in 2022 to an estimated $35 billion in 2025. EU member states together spent €418 billion on defence that year, so Ukraine’s edge is the speed of its innovation. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

The tempting conclusion is that a country able to produce such technology under these pressures can build anything Europe needs, including air defence, if the money is there. Indeed, Kyiv has called on partners to help build ‘the arsenal of the free world’ with Ukraine. However, operational effectiveness should not be confused with industrial capacity. 

Know-how is not the main constraint: Ukraine inherited much of the Soviet Union’s missile-design base, and its companies are now developing ballistic and anti-ballistic missiles alongside unmanned systems. 

The binding constraints are instead access to capital, production capacity, industrial facilities that are vulnerable to Russian attacks, and the availability of specialist components, particularly advanced electronics and seekers.

Of these, finance is the most immediate concern. The head of Ukraine’s Council of Defence Industry has said that manufacturers are operating at around 40 per cent of their potential capacity because the government is not placing enough orders. That suggests that additional funding could quickly unlock production potential. 

However, Europe’s requirements go beyond volume. Advanced air defence, particularly against ballistic missiles, depends on complex radar and sensor networks, high-end interceptors and industrial supply chains that require substantial investment and sustained development. Ukraine’s experience can inform European capability development. But it does not remove the need for Europe to build and maintain such capabilities itself.

The limits of a supplier relationship

There are other limitations on purchasing from Ukraine. Kyiv’s export framework is designed to protect its own forces. Companies may export only if they can also fulfil Ukrainian government contracts. Exports carry no intellectual property rights. And re-export requires Kyiv’s approval and attracts a 20 per cent tax.  

Even the drones built at the first Ukrainian joint venture in Germany are currently allocated to Ukraine’s armed forces. These are rational choices for a country fighting for its survival. But they mean that in a crisis, European governments could not assume Ukrainian output would be available for their own requirements, at least until Kyiv’s rules adapted.

A ceasefire would raise a different problem extending beyond supply-chain security. Ukraine’s advantage is tied to the operational environment in which its firms develop and test equipment. A settlement would necessarily reduce the operational feedback, procurement incentives and pressure that drive innovation. European planning should not assume that the wartime model will persist, or that Ukraine’s production priorities will stay aligned with Europe’s.

Closer cooperation also carries political risk: Moscow’s reaction to Destinus fits a pattern of embassy statements labelling Dutch support for Ukraine as participation in the conflict. European governments should anticipate diplomatic coercion and hostile activity directed against facilities, personnel and supply chains associated with Ukrainian defence production. Russia has already named European firms producing drones for Ukraine as potential targets. In August, an explosive-laden drone was found beside a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport, an attack Germany has since attributed to Russia. Such hybrid attacks could make some European governments more cautious about hosting joint production, underlining the importance of protecting facilities, personnel and supply chains.

From procurement to partnership

The European Commission’s proposed €45 billion loan to Ukraine for 2027, the second half of the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, including €31.7 billion for defence, provides an opportunity to shape cooperation. The allocation of these funds will have long-term consequences beyond Ukraine’s immediate military requirements. 

Funding can support Ukrainian production for domestic use, establish joint ventures on European territory, or, where EU rules allow a derogation, finance procurement from established suppliers outside Europe, including the United States. 

Buying Ukrainian output sustains Ukraine’s defence. And buying from outside Europe fills immediate gaps. But only joint ventures build enduring capacity across Europe. Ukraine’s immediate needs, particularly for air defence this winter, must remain central to European assistance. But joint ventures are where support and European industrial development can converge, and where a meaningful share of the package should be directed.

The partnership should rest on a division of labour that draws on what Ukraine’s circumstances have produced. The war has given Ukraine’s defence industry what European nations cannot match during peacetime: urgency, a tolerance for failure, and feedback loops that are measured in days. 

Reinforced by Kyiv stripping out procurement, testing and regulatory barriers, Ukraine’s industry benefits from low-cost mass production and rapid iteration under pressure. That has delivered interceptor drones and long-range strike at a pace and cost that European procurement has, to date, struggled to match. 

Partnership offers the rest of Europe a way to learn from Ukraine’s experience of rapid development and operational feedback, while reinforcing the need to reform Europe’s procurement systems. Ukraine is already offering foreign firms the chance to test equipment in near-combat conditions alongside frontline units, through its state-backed Brave1 defence-tech cluster, and to pair with Ukrainian manufacturers for co-production. European states should take up that offer as partners rather than customers. 

European states and companies, in turn, bring radar and sensor technology, high-end interceptors, sovereign space-based communications, capital, and production sites beyond the reach of Russian missiles. 

Joint ventures and licensed production can bring these together, but only if they involve genuine technology transfer, shared research, integrated supply chains, and appropriate allocation priority when the future security picture shifts. Ukrainian reporting has described the German joint venture as closer to a showcase than the start of a systematic process, whereas Destinus reports output approaching 300 Ruta missiles a month.

Moving from individual projects to an enduring framework will require predictable multi-year financing and agreements on intellectual property that give Ukrainian and European manufacturers the confidence to invest together.

European leaders should therefore ask not only how much to spend on Ukraine, but how that spending can future-proof collective European security and capability. Treating Ukraine as a source of weapons risks creating a dependency that becomes visible only when European security is next under pressure. Building shared industrial capacity would strengthen Ukraine’s defence and Europe’s resilience at the same time.

title: Spain’s election could see Europe’s far-right ‘firewall’ begin to fall apart
author: thilton.drupal
description:
Spain’s election could see Europe’s far-right ‘firewall’ begin to fall apart Expert comment thilton.drupal 23 November 2026

Polls suggest the Spanish election could produce a coalition of the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party, with consequences far beyond Madrid.

Spain votes on Sunday 29 November in a snap general election called by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. Most polls suggest the conservative opposition Partido Popular (PP), led by Alberto Feijóo, will be the largest party but fall short of a majority itself. They also suggest that together with the far-right Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, the right-wing bloc would have a combined majority in the 350-seat parliament. 

As of 22 November, Convergent Opinion’s MRP poll put the two parties on a combined 186 seats, 10 above the 176 needed. 

It is illegal in Spain to publish polls in the week leading up to the election, which is when data suggests that voters typically decide who to vote for, leaving poll watchers in the dark during the final straight. This may aid the left-wing bloc as voters consider how best to tactical vote against the right. 

Sánchez has been clear that the only route to victory for the left is high mobilization – with the prime minister targeting a turnout of 75 per cent. Although the Socialists have gained ground in the campaign, the gap between blocs may be too large to overturn without such extraordinary high turnout.

A PP-Vox coalition government seems the most likely outcome. In this instance, Vox would not just lend its votes from outside government. On current polling it would win between 55 and 69 seats, close to a third of the right-wing bloc. This would be enough to claim ministries and shape policy. 

However, it remains to be seen whether Vox choses to pursue its objectives from within government or to exert pressure on a minority Feijoo government. Until now, the PP and Vox have governed together only in regional and local government. A national coalition would give Vox a say in Spain’s foreign policy for the first time. It would also be the first time the far right has been in government in Spain since it became a democratic country. 

Elsewhere in Europe, Finland, Sweden and the Netherlands have all brought the far right into government or into formal support arrangements. But Spain is the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy and, under Sánchez, has been the most outspoken progressive government among the EU’s large states. 

If Vox is brought into government, Spain will become the test case for what happens when Europe’s centre right drops its barrier to the far right at the national level – referred to as the ‘firewall’ in Germany. It will have direct consequences for Spain’s foreign policy and wider European politics. 

Divided over Europe

The deepest divide between the two potential coalition parties is over Europe itself. The PP belongs to the European People’s Party, the group that leads the EU institutions. In 2024, Vox left the European Conservatives and Reformists group and joined the Patriots for Europe, the far more Eurosceptic group that was founded by Viktor Orbán.

On trade, Vox calls the EU-Mercosur trade agreement a ‘betrayal’ of Spanish farmers and attacks the PP for supporting it. If a coalition is formed, Feijóo will need to decide if he will defend a deal in Brussels that his coalition partner back home has virulently rejected. 

On Ukraine, Feijóo’s PP supports Kyiv in line with the mainstream European centre right position. However, when US President Trump clashed with Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy in the White House in 2025, Abascal took Trump’s side and attacked the European leaders backing Kyiv. Vox denies being pro-Russian, but Abascal has previously sought to blame Europe for financing the war in Ukraine and his party has repeatedly abstained on resolutions in the European Parliament. 

Morocco, migration and Gibraltar 

Vox’s manifesto makes ‘remigration’ a central promise, borrowing the term from Germany’s AfD. Yet Spain cannot easily control migration without Morocco’s cooperation. The PP’s Feijóo had pledged to make Morocco his first foreign visit as prime minister, but his tone has hardened since the Ceuta border crisis in the summer. In last week’s televised debate, he called the crisis an ‘invasion’, taking a far more hostile line towards Rabat than Sánchez. Vox, for its part, has vowed to militarize the border – something unlikely to please Rabat. 

Related work

The Ceuta border crisis heaps pressure on Spain’s Sánchez government – and European unity

On Gibraltar, a PP-Vox government would inherit the UK-EU treaty, which has applied provisionally since 15 July. Vox calls it  ‘illegal, illegitimate and unjust’ and has pledged to ‘recover Spanish sovereignty over the Rock of Gibraltar.’ Vox will likely press to reopen the issue, and Feijóo would have to choose between a dispute with London and Brussels and a dispute with his own coalition partner. 

For British EU ‘rejoiners’, this will be a reminder that the bloc they hope to rejoin is changing. Any future UK application would need the agreement of every member state, including Spain. Other elections across Europe in the next 12 months may see other far-right parties come to power and support Vox’s position, potentially complicating any negotiations if the UK does decide to rejoin the EU. 

Part of a wider contest

Foreign policy has been important in this election. Sánchez has told voters that the world is watching Spain and has made opposition to Trump central to his politics. 

On 16 November, Sánchez welcomed President Lula to Madrid just weeks after he won the Brazilian election. Sánchez’s supporters have been buoyed by Lula’s victory, as well as by the Democrats winning big in the US midterms. This came after Orbán lost power in Hungary in April.

On the other side, Argentina’s President Javier Milei used a visit to Madrid in October to call Sánchez an ‘unpresentable dictator’ at a right-wing rally. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni sent a message of support to the same rally, as did Marine Le Pen and Orbán. Elon Musk has called Sánchez ‘a tyrant and a traitor’ over Spain’s plan to ban social media for under-16s. 

Spain’s election will therefore be important in setting the tone for an upcoming crowded electoral year in Europe. In April 2027, France elects a president, with the far-right Rassemblement National’s Le Pen leading the polls. Finland, Estonia and Greece will also hold parliamentary elections, while Poland and Italy will vote by the end of the year. 

International impact

Centre-right parties elsewhere in Europe also have to decide whether to work with the far right or not. In Germany, the far-right AfD won 44 per cent in Saxony-Anhalt in September, and the centre-right CDU’s firewall is under more strain than ever. In France, Les Républicains have ruled out a pact with the Rassemblement National for 2027, but the call from the mayor of Nice to work with Le Pen’s camp suggested some are unwilling to toe that line.

Related work

The AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt marks a turning point for Germany – but perspective is important

A divided left is a central factor in the potential victories of the far right. In Spain, the far-left Podemos and the left-wing Frente Amplio failed to agree a joint list in October. Podemos has been polling between 1 and 2 per cent – in Spain’s electoral system this means most of their vote will be wasted. In fact, Podemos has since spent much of the campaign attacking Sánchez and the Socialists, which could also depress left-wing turnout. 

The pattern is not dissimilar elsewhere. In the UK, Labour lost ground to the Greens in May’s local elections. In Germany, the SPD has fallen to 15 per cent according to the latest poll from YouGov, equal to the Greens’ 15 per cent, with Die Linke (‘The Left’) on 10 per cent.

Given an increasingly fragmented electorate, centre-right parties may need the far right to govern, as Feijóo likely will now. If a PP-Vox government holds together and keeps Spain close to the European mainstream, it will be cited as proof that the firewall was never needed. But if it splits over Ukraine, Morocco or Brussels, it will strengthen the case for keeping the firewall. Sunday’s election is therefore important not just to Spain, but to Europe and the world.

title: It’s Time to Settle With Russia
author: Michael C. Desch
description: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

description: Proposals to shorten the workweek are back on the policy agenda in Europe and the US. This column draws on France’s 35-hour reform to assess two central promises: work-sharing and productivity gains. Lower-skill workers bore most of the costs.

description: Cross-country data on what governments do are scarce. This column introduces the Global Fiscal Actions dataset, a new quarterly database of tax and spending measures in 142 countries since 1990, constructed using large language models to classify fiscal actions by their direction, instrument, motivation, implementation status, and size. Fiscal actions are frequent, typically small, predominantly expansionary, and spending-based, although fiscal sustainability is the most cited motivation. Over the past decade, spending actions have become less procyclical, while tax actions remain acyclical. Fiscal actions are synchronised across countries only during global recessions, and multipliers vary more within income groups than between them.

title: Researcher choices matter: Synthetic controls and California’s $20 fast-food minimum wage
author: Jeffrey Clemens, Olivia Edwards, Jonathan Meer, Joshua Nguyen
description: Studies of California's $20 fast-food minimum wage disagree about whether it reduced employment. Much of the disagreement arises from a substantial number of seemingly innocuous researcher decisions on comparison group construction. This column reports the results of 1,440 plausible synthetic-control specifications. More than 96% of the estimates show job losses, but the range is wide. Estimates that imply no effect sit in the tail of the distribution. By contrast, the estimates that arise from simple comparisons between California and the rest of the US imply an employment decline of around 3% and land near the distribution’s centre. The authors argue that results should be shown across a range of defensible choices.

title: Export controls are broader than you think, but they buy more security with coordination
author: Jingting Fan, Kyle Handley, Nuno Limão
description: China, the EU, and the US are all expanding their export controls on items with both civilian and military applications. This column combines data on US exports with a quantitative trade model to examine the effects of export controls on dual-use goods. When the US and its allies impose controls together, target countries’ imports of controlled goods fall 5.7 times as much as under unilateral US controls. Coordination delivers a larger security gain for the US, measured as the rise in US real military spending relative to target countries, at a similar cost to civilians in terms of incomes and prices of goods.

title: Locked out: Drivers and consequences of housing affordability pressures in Europe
author: Robert Beyer, Nina Biljanovska, Alexandra Fotiou, Morgan Maneely, Frederik Toscani
description: Rising housing costs have intensified affordability crises across Europe. This column examines the drivers of this growth, its distributional effects on households, and implications for labour mobility. While the pre-global financial crisis rise in house prices was largely driven by credit supply, housing supply constraints have become a more important driver of prices in recent years. Housing affordability pressures are highly uneven across location, housing tenure, income groups, and the level of urbanisation, and have widened income and wealth gaps between owners and renters. Beyond distributional concerns, declining affordability also has adverse consequences for labour allocation and efficiency.

title: Will Saddam Haftar be Libya’s next president?
author: thilton.drupal
description:
Will Saddam Haftar be Libya’s next president? Expert comment thilton.drupal 20 November 2026

The son of commander Khalifa Haftar has consolidated his position as heir apparent and expanded his influence. But his pursuit of the presidency could bring Libya back into conflict.

Saddam Haftar, the son of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF) commander Khalifa Haftar, has recently visited several foreign capitals in an apparent attempt to boost his international standing. This has been seen as part of a concerted push to become Libya’s next president.

This effort will define Libya’s politics for the coming months. It has huge implications for the country’s political future amid a US-led push for a national government that would unify Libya’s two rival administrations: the LAAF-controlled administration in eastern Libya and the Government of National Unity (GNU) in Tripoli. Strong opposition to Saddam’s goals in western Libya also means that the risk of conflict is increasing.

Saddam becomes heir apparent

For many years, there have been questions over Khalifa Haftar’s succession. The assumption has been that Haftar, 83, would remain in direct control of the LAAF while alive. It was speculated that the LAAF could fragment without Haftar, given the LAAF’s status as a hybrid of a military institution and a family enterprise.  

However, in recent years, Haftar has increasingly taken a back seat as his sons Saddam, Khaled, Belgassim and al-Sadiq have come to the fore. Their rise became clearer after the failure of the LAAF to capture Tripoli in 2020, which led Haftar to reassess his approach. Over subsequent years, the LAAF was restructured. Its forces were placed under the command of Saddam and Khaled, who gained responsibility for land forces and security units respectively. 

Meanwhile, Belgassim developed strong networks and influence in political circles. He was instrumental in the formation of a new government that sought to replace the sitting GNU in Tripoli. In 2023, Belgassim also assumed the helm of the Libyan Development and Reconstruction Programme, formed after floods killed several thousand people in Derna, which provided a new narrative of development for the Haftar family.

However, Khalifa’s appointment of Saddam as deputy general commander in August 2025 sealed his position as heir apparent. Saddam has become the most powerful of the sons through not just his military position, but also his alleged increasing influence via proxies over the oil and gas and banking sectors in eastern Libya.

The Boulos initiative

Saddam’s rise is important in the context of the push for a unified government in Libya. This has been led by Massad Boulos, the US Special Advisor for Africa and the Middle East. Under Boulos’ plan, a unified government would be formed as part of a deal between the two ruling families: the Haftars, who control eastern Libya, and the Dabaibas, who control the Tripoli-based GNU.

While the US has not publicized the parameters of the deal, insiders have said that Saddam Haftar would become a member of the Presidency Council, the three-person body whose chairman is Libya’s de facto head of state. The Dabaiba family would retain the prime minister’s post.

Related work

Why US plans for power-sharing in Libya will not work

Negotiating processes had previously focused on seeking agreement between Libya’s fractious institutions: the chronically divided House of Representatives in eastern Libya and the Tripoli-based High State Council. But the US plan has broken with this formula, instead seeking agreement between the Haftars and the Dabaibas. The first agreement made through this channel was a deal on budgetary spending in April 2026.

Subsequently, the United Nations adapted to the new format. The UN Mission’s ‘4+4’ committee brought together a combination of representatives from the GNU, LAAF, the House of Representatives and the High State Council. The 4+4 reached agreement on a roadmap for national elections in August.

This pivot towards negotiations being between the LAAF and the GNU – essentially between the emissaries of Saddam Haftar and the Dabaibas – is more significant than the content of the agreement. It officially places Saddam’s LAAF General Command as a negotiating party with parity with the internationally recognized GNU.  

Path to the presidency?

Buoyed by these diplomatic advances, Saddam has recently made significant moves to expand his influence.

The ousting of the longtime speaker of the House of Representatives in October – and his replacement with a figure known for his support for the LAAF – is widely understood to have been orchestrated by Saddam.

Shortly after, the House of Representatives moved to ratify a controversial memorandum of understanding with Turkey over the recognition of drilling rights in the eastern Mediterranean. Insiders have said privately that Saddam pushed for this move, which angered Egypt and European countries, presumably with the aim of securing Ankara’s support for his push for the presidency in return.

Then, on 26 October, the governor of the Central Bank of Libya was replaced, reportedly due to a private agreement between the Haftars and the Dabaibas. The Central Bank holds a critical place in the management of Libya’s economy, overseeing the distribution of foreign currency and dinar payments that are so crucial to Libya’s leaders.

That same week, Saddam was in Turkey for talks with the GNU on military reunification.

Alongside strengthening his influence over important institutions in Libya, Saddam has consequently emerged as the apparent partner of preference for the some of the most influential international actors. He is seen as someone who can get things done and maintain order in comparison to the messy picture of contested power in western Libya.

The enduring Haftar ‘problem’ and the risk of conflict

Saddam is now central to any political effort to reunify the country. His ambitions to enter Tripoli are widely known. Those familiar with the security sector in the capital note that local allies of Saddam are seeking to prepare the ground for his arrival.

But opposition to – and mistrust of – Saddam in western Libya remains strong, especially in key constituencies such as the city of Misrata. This has not been helped by the uncovering of a sleeper cell, allegedly linked to the LAAF, that was accused of seeking to cause damage to oil and gas infrastructure in the city of Zawiya in August.

Many doubt that Saddam is willing to share power. It therefore seems no meaningful guarantees can be provided to Saddam’s opponents to reassure them. Western Libyan actors would like to separate the discussion of military reunification from political reunification as a result.

Consequently, while the Dabaiba family may be willing to cut deals to retain a modus vivendi with Saddam, it is highly unlikely to sign a deal making Saddam president. This is evident in the fact that no deal has yet been reached, despite intensive efforts over months by Boulos.

This, in turn, creates a problem. It is not clear how Saddam’s rapid rise and apparent aspirations for president can be squared with his opponents’ steadfast opposition to him. And they are unlikely to go anywhere, considering that the Dabaibas are entrenched in power too.

This fundamental difference runs deeper than the Boulos initiative. As one source in the security sector told me: even if there were elections, Saddam would not accept the results if he loses, and his opponents would not accept the results if he wins.

If Saddam continues to push for the presidency, Libya therefore faces a heightened risk of conflict. Many of his opponents would seemingly prefer the messy situation in Tripoli to prevail over a new order that could ultimately end up squarely under Saddam’s control. But, given the strength of international support building behind Saddam’s campaign, their options are narrowing.

title: The ICJ’s Myanmar finding shifts the dial – a little – on the grounds for a guilty verdict in a genocide case
author: jon.wallace
description:
The ICJ’s Myanmar finding shifts the dial – a little – on the grounds for a guilty verdict in a genocide case Expert comment jon.wallace 20 November 2026

The Court’s unusually split decision seems to adjust how intent to destroy a group ‘in whole or in part’ is established.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the highest court in the world, has ruled that Myanmar is guilty of genocide. According to the Court, the ‘clearance’ campaign by the Myanmar military against its Rohingya minority of 2017 was aimed at the destruction, in whole or in part, of that community. The finding in this case, which was brought before the Court by the Gambia in 2019, will reverberate far beyond Myanmar and its immediate environment.

The ICJ’s previous genocide cases

The Rohingya are a mainly Muslim ethnic group that has been excluded from Myanmar citizenship and discriminated against for decades. In the wake of attacks by terrorist groups against the military in 2016, some 10,000 Rohingya were killed, and over 85 per cent of its population of around 850,000 were displaced from Myanmar over the following year in a campaign of killings, rape and the burning of villages.

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

The ICJ has established a very high bar for confirming that genocide has occurred. Several cases, including those brought by Croatia against Serbia and Sudan against the UAE, have been unsuccessful. 

Others are still ongoing, addressing the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, Ukraine and the Russian Federation, and Gaza.

Only once before, in relation to the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of 8,000 men and boys in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has the ICJ confirmed genocide. But controversially, it failed to attribute the atrocity to its alleged author, the Republic of Serbia (then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia) under Slobodan Milosevic.

This new decision of the Court moves the dial ever so slightly, reducing the legal hurdles on the way towards a finding of genocide. 

The grounds for a finding of genocide

According to the Genocide Convention of 1948, genocide requires three elements. 

First, it must be directed against a protected group, defined by national, ethnic, racial or religious characteristics. Second, there must be prohibited acts directed against members of the group. This includes killings, causing serious bodily or mental harm, inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of the group, or measures intended to prevent births or forcibly transferring children to another group. 

But critically, even if a pattern of such practices is clearly evident, this must be carried by the specific intent to destroy the group as such ‘in whole or in part’ – the third element.

This may seem odd. If the result is the destruction of the group, one might argue that this should suffice to constitute genocide. Such conduct would clearly amount to a crime against humanity and other severe violations of human rights and humanitarian law. However, in defining what is sometimes called ‘the crime of crimes,’ the Genocide Convention imposes this additional criterion of specific intent. 

Of course, that is difficult to prove. States no longer record their decision to commit genocide in a formal document, as Hitler’s government did in the famous 1942 Wannsee Protocol, which planned the complete destruction of Europe’s Jewish population. 

Without such formal documentation, proof of the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part must be inferred from the nature of a systematic campaign of killing and other acts proscribed by the Genocide Convention that are directed at a defined population segment.

Previously, the Court asserted that such an inference can only be made if this pattern cannot be explained by any reason other than the intention to commit genocide. 

In its defence, Myanmar offered several alternative grounds to explain the nature of its armed campaign. It referred to the need to mount a counter-terrorism effort following attacks by rebel movements in Rakhine province, where most Rohingya used to reside. However, in view of the Court, this motivation would not explain the pattern of brutal attacks against the civilian population.

The Court also considered whether Myanmar’s conduct might simply have been directed at the forcible displacement of the Rohingya, rather than their destruction in whole or in part. This alone would be a serious international crime, but it would not quite amount to genocide.

However, the Court looked at the overall context of the long-standing campaign against the Rohingya – including discrimination, hate speech, the nature of the military operation and other culpable acts systematically targeting this group and affecting its ‘foundations’ or existence.

In broadening this overall context, and relying on the totality of the evidence, rather than just the well attested reports of individual atrocities, the Court was able to assert that the intent to commit genocide was the only reasonable inference that could be drawn.

The effect on other cases

This outcome will concern some governments involved in other ongoing cases regarding genocide. 

Ukraine brought a case before the ICJ in 2022, asking the Court to confirm that it had not committed genocide against Russian-speakers on its territory – a central claim made by Russia to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that year. 

In another case, the DRC is alleging that Rwanda is involved in genocide conducted on its territory. In a further action, Nicaragua is alleging that Germany shares responsibility for the alleged genocide in Gaza due to its supply of arms to Israel. 

The Court’s Myanmar judgement may impact these cases. But international attention is mainly focused on the case’s implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. 

In an initial, provisional phase of the case, the Court found that there may be a plausible case of genocide in relation to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

Counsel for Israel and South Africa, along with the over 20 others states that have intervened in that case, will now assess the Court’s finding and ask: what would the outcome be if the matrix of factors applied by the ICJ in the Myanmar case were applied to Israel’s armed campaign in Gaza? Would this exercise demonstrate that the intent to commit genocide is the only reasonable explanation for the character of that campaign?

Related work

South Africa’s genocide case against Israel: The International Court of Justice explained

The key clauses in the Myanmar judgement were adopted by an unusually divided Court, by a majority of 9 to 6. The ICJ decides according to the applicable law, not the politics involved in a given situation. But its decision will probably be criticized by some as having lowered the threshold for the identification of genocide, perhaps with a view to confirming the relevance of the Court and of the international rule of law. International law has been largely disregarded in many recent conflicts – especially its humanitarian provisions. 

On the other hand, those opposing the Court’s finding might be accused of trying to prevent a precedent being established when it comes to evaluating the Gaza case.

In addition to political controversy, the case raises another important issue: A third state, The Gambia – which is not involved in Myanmar’s conflict – managed to obtain a ruling in favour of a dispossessed and internationally disenfranchised minority group located a continent away. 

The Gambia brought the action with the support of the Organization of the Islamic Conference and senior international lawyers, adopting a kind of international public service role in defence of the international public order. It confirmed that all states have a firm legal interest in compliance with that rule by all other states, and that parties to the Genocide Convention can bring a case to the Court in defence of the prohibition of genocide. 

The Court even considered that in this case between The Gambia and Myanmar, it has the authority to rule on the entitlement of the Rohingya as the ultimate beneficiaries of the obligation to prevent genocide to restitution and compensation from their own government. In this way, it has reasserted and indeed extended its role of guardian of the international rule of law at a time of challenge to global order.

title: First Impressions Matter: Measuring and Correcting Position Bias in Business Environment Estimates
author: Aga, Gemechu Ayana
description: Estimating the constraints in the business environment guides development policy and allocation of resources. title: What does COP31 reveal about the geopolitics of climate change?
author: jon.wallace
description:
What does COP31 reveal about the geopolitics of climate change? Expert comment jon.wallace 19 November 2026

Some claim COPs take place in a bubble. But the summits say much about the interplay between climate policy, the energy transition, and the shifts underway in international relations.

Today, much of the political right in developed countries rejects efforts to combat climate change. Even leaders nominally of the centre and left are deprioritizing efforts to reduce emissions. Meanwhile many corporations are dropping their net zero targets. And fossil fuel companies are scrapping or scaling back their low-carbon divisions. 

It might seem strange, then, that this year’s COP31 climate change conference in Turkey attracted more people than ever. A record 93,000 participants as well as 77 heads of state and governments registered to attend. 

A COP headcount is a crude proxy for the global salience of climate policy. Nevertheless, it is worth asking: Is COP31 taking place in a bubble that is disconnected from geopolitical realities? Or does it indicate how climate change and the energy transition are simultaneously reflecting and influencing seismic geopolitical shifts?

Detached from reality?

When the first COP summit took place in Bonn in 1995, the world was vastly different. Climate-fuelled disasters were still theoretical. Practical, affordable low-carbon technology was a distant dream. The United States appeared to be the world’s only superpower, its alliances assured. 

Want to hear more on the path to a secure energy transition?

Join us at our climate and energy summit, where policymakers and industry leaders tackle the toughest questions on climate and energy security.

All of this has changed. Yet many negotiating positions at COP remain frozen in time. Entrenched definitions of ‘developed’ and ‘developing’ countries shape expectations of who is responsible for providing climate finance. 

That is despite some of the latter group – notably the Gulf states – now being amongst the world’s wealthiest on a per capita basis. Developing countries call for knowledge and technology transfer from developed countries, even though it is China – considered a developing country – that is overwhelmingly dominant in the field. 

Meanwhile the level of ambition seems at odds with the reality of an urgent, present climate crisis. For instance, the flagship electrification target proposed by hosts Australia and Turkey at COP31 will not require that the electricity generated must come from low carbon sources, despite the clear cost advantage in doing so. Such a stipulation is basically off the table in Antalya, a consequence of the continued influence of fossil fuel interests.

COPs do therefore, to some extent, take place in a bubble. But they are vital in understanding the interplay of climate change with real-world geopolitics.

‘Developed’ countries

The countries considered developed when the climate regime was established in the early 1990s are today on the back foot. In some, domestic consensus has eroded, making it more difficult for politicians and officials to negotiate climate change at the global level. 

The most extreme example is the United States. The US is not represented by a delegation at COP31, with President Donald Trump having formally withdrawn the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025 and the underlying UN convention in 2026. This followed a period of energetic US reengagement on international climate policy under President Joe Biden, following the US withdrawal from Paris in 2017 during President Trump’s first term.  

This whipsaw climate policy is influenced by the US’s superpower showdown with China. That competition would ideally encourage a ‘race-to-the-top’ on low-carbon technology, as it briefly did under President Biden with the Inflation Reduction Act. But policy is also influenced by the US’s newfound position as the world’s leading oil and gas producer. President Trump’s ‘energy dominance’ strategy has sought to capitalize on that position while dismissing climate science and rejecting renewable energy.

The EU, traditionally among the most ambitious of the blocs at COP, has dialled down its expectations for COP31 – in no small part due to the absence of the US. The EU’s top climate diplomat, Wopke Hoestra, called for a narrow focus on the electrification target, while dismissing any further talks on finance as ‘dead in the water’. 

Europe’s political class is also distracted, not least by the Russian threat. The World Leaders’ Summit in Antalya was relatively light on European leadership, most of whom attended a security-focused European Political Community meeting in Dublin instead. 

Canada and the UK, positioning themselves as responsible ‘middle powers’, issued a joint statement at COP31 affirming their commitment to climate finance goals and announcing new funding pledges. But this international positioning is paired with domestic retreat. Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Canada has dismantled climate policies and committed public funds to new fossil fuel infrastructure. Under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the UK has approved new drilling for gas and is considering weakening electric vehicle targets.

Burnham did attend the COP leaders’ summit. But in his address, he said that the consensus on climate had ‘gone’. This betrays a UK-centric perspective. Cross-party support for climate action has indeed collapsed in Westminster. But a record share of the global population (75 per cent) considers climate change a serious threat.

‘Developing’ countries

The countries considered developing within the international climate regime include varying economy sizes and climate vulnerabilities. But some broad trends exist among them.

First, many are treating the new low-carbon economy as a major growth and development opportunity. Countries in South-East Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and Latin America are rolling out renewables at a rate which will soon match or exceed that of their rich-world peers. Saudi Arabia, which has long blocked progress at COPs (and reprised this role in Antalya) used COP31 to announce a major wind and solar energy deal with hosts Turkey.

Secondly, developing countries intend to hold developed countries to their commitments, as the world experiences climate impacts with ever greater frequency and severity. Financing climate adaptation and compensating loss and damage is becoming central at the talks and were repeatedly referenced at the Leaders’ Summit. 

However, very few developed countries have renewed their financial pledges after they expired in 2025. That is despite previously pledging to lead efforts to scale up climate finance to $300 billion by 2035. 

China

And then there is Beijing. China is, by some distance, the country responsible for the largest share of greenhouse gas emissions (29.5 per cent in 2025). But it is also deploying low-carbon technologies at breathtaking speed and scale. 

Related work

What does China’s new Five-Year Plan mean for the climate?

It is exporting its solar panels, batteries, EVs and more, framing this as a central part of its contribution to global climate efforts. That is not without justification: the country’s clean tech exports in 2026 will cut emissions equivalent to what Brazil emits in a year. 

Here is where climate and geopolitics truly meet. Developed countries are struggling to honour their international climate finance commitments and decelerating their domestic efforts (or in the case of the US, repudiating both). Meanwhile, China, which styles itself as the leader of the developing countries, is supplying the means to transition, and providing huge investment in clean tech manufacturing abroad.

This is despite concerns that China is part of an effort, along with Saudi Arabia, Russia, India and Kenya, to delay work on crucial climate science. 

Separating the signal from the noise

When the COP process began in the 1990s, the goal was simple: to fix climate change. These days, very few would argue it can manage that on its own. 

When the dust settles, COP31 will have provided us with a distorted, confusing and ultimately dissatisfying representation of collective efforts to address climate change – as it always has. 

But focusing on conference outcomes alone ignores real world progress on the energy transition, and how climate change continues to shape and be shaped by geopolitical shifts. 

The Iran war has made low-carbon technology more attractive in many parts of the world. The traditional leaders of the Global North are seen by the Global South as reluctant to meet their commitments to tackle a climate crisis that is increasingly disruptive. China is receiving an ever-warmer reception, through its clean technology, its investments, and its relative stability as an international climate actor. 

COP31 may conclude this week, but the geopolitics of climate change and the energy transition are only getting started.

title: Closing the Energy Efficiency Gap: Unlocking Private-Sector Investment in Poland and Romania
author: World Bank
description: This report examines the persistent gap between the significant potential for energy-efficiency improvements and actual private-sector investment in Europe, drawing on detailed analysis of Poland and Romania. It finds that stronger energy efficiency can improve firms’ competitiveness, energy security, and emissions performance, but investment remains constrained by limited firm capabilities, weak pipelines of bankable projects, low borrower demand, restrictive investment criteria, financing gaps, and poorly targeted or administered public support. The analysis shows that moving underperforming firms to median sector-level energy efficiency could reduce energy consumption and emissions by an estimated 38 to 44 percent, while increasing profitability by only 2 to 6 percent, highlighting the large social and environmental benefits relative to private returns. SMEs face particular challenges in identifying, assessing, and financing energy-efficiency opportunities, while commercial-bank lending for such projects remains limited. Based on findings from Poland and Romania, the report recommends strengthening regulatory governance, redesigning public financial support toward more predictable and repayable instruments, improving energy audits and follow-through, using green public procurement to stimulate demand, mobilizing private capital through green lending and risk-sharing mechanisms, and strengthening firms’ technical capabilities and awareness. Together, these measures can help make energy efficiency a scalable and investable business proposition while directing public resources toward sectors and market failures where they can deliver the greatest economic, energy-security, and emissions benefits.

title: Connecting Rural Areas: Roads and Structural Transformation in Mali
author: Mesple-Somps, Sandrine
description: This study examines how road investments affected structural transformation in rural Mali using an exhaustive panel of localities constructed from census micro-data and a difference-indifferences identification strategy. Between 1998 and 2009, gaining paved-road access increased a rural locality’s population by 13.5 percent, the male share by 1 percentage point, and the share of non-agricultural employment by 6.7 percentage points. Population gains were concentrated in localities near cities, while non-agricultural employment increased in remote areas, suggesting population growth without structural transformation near cities, but sectoral convergence in remote localities. New or upgraded road connections were also associated with improved local welfare.

title: When Aspirational Videos Meet Socio-Emotional Skills Training: Experimental Evidence from a Youth Employment Program in Côte d’Ivoire
author: Rouanet, Léa
description: Socio-emotional skills training is increasingly embedded in youth employment programs, often alongside aspirational content, yet evidence on how these components interact remains limited. This paper evaluates a randomized controlled trial with 6,023 urban out-of-school youth in Côte d'Ivoire. Participants were assigned to a control group or a multi-component employment program whose socio-emotional modules emphasized either intrapersonal or interpersonal skills, and were further randomized to one of two sets of aspirational videos or no video. Impacts differed substantially by gender. For women, both training packages without a video improved labor market participation, and the intrapersonal arm additionally improved sexual and reproductive health, raising contraceptive use and reducing the likelihood of being pregnant or breastfeeding. For most outcomes, equality between the two treatment packages cannot be rejected. For men, the effects were limited. Adding either set of videos largely eliminated women's labor market and reproductive gains, although the videos on shared-responsibilities were also associated with reductions in specific forms of violence among women and with stronger social networks among men.  The paper finds little evidence of changes in socio-emotional skills, aspirations, or gender attitudes. Qualitative evidence suggests improvements in confidence, planning, and day-to-day decision-making, while the videos appear to have increased the salience of risks and constraints facing young women. The results suggest that a multi-component skills program can improve women's economic and reproductive outcomes, but also that seemingly complementary motivational content commonly used to reinforce training may erode these gains when increasing the salience of barriers that women remain unable to overcome.

title: Yalta this is not: The Xi–Trump–Putin meeting is China’s show and America’s loss
author: jon.wallace
description:
Yalta this is not: The Xi–Trump–Putin meeting is China’s show and America’s loss Expert comment jon.wallace 18 November 2026

The meeting offers little for US interests, risk for Ukraine – and a sobering image for Europe and other countries. 

President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and President Vladimir Putin might be tempted to accept the comparisons being drawn between their coming talks in Shenzhen on Thursday and the Yalta summit of 1945. There, US President Franklin Delano Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin set out the post-war peace, carving up the world between them – though the end of the British Empire was already inevitable. 

But this week’s meeting is no Yalta. It is showmanship. Any deals to be done are small – and they are all in China’s favour, unless Trump decides to side with Russia over Ukraine. 

For the rest of the world, particularly the UK and European Union, the display is a reminder of the urgent need to shore up regional alliances, the United Nations, and the rule of international law where possible. 

The players

Trump has most to lose from going to this summit. The US would have been better off had he not gone. Perhaps he was attracted by the image of standing shoulder to shoulder with two authoritarian leaders he seems to admire – more than he does the leaders of the US’s democratic allies. Perhaps it was the possibility of taking part in a Yalta-like exercise in shaping the world. 

If that was his judgement, it is wrong. For a start, unlike the Yalta photograph of 1945 (where the three leaders were seated, concealing the fact that the ailing Roosevelt needed a wheelchair) the US president will not be placed in the centre. That role will go to Xi, as host. But that positioning will also reflect the reality. Xi is the leader of the power with the least need of concessions from the others. 

Besides matters of presentation, by attending this meeting Trump surrenders yet again what has been since 1945 the US’s strongest card: that it has been the ‘leader of the free world’, upholding the rights of democracies and acting as a beacon to all those who espouse those principles. Instead, Trump carries the banner of ‘Might Makes Right’ to the summit. 

Unlike Trump, Putin has much to gain from this meeting. Russia is no superpower. Its economy is dwindling, with 40 per cent of production diverted to his war in Ukraine. With this summit in mind, Ukraine this week bombed Putin’s prized Kerch bridge to Crimea, built in 2014 after Russia’s invasion of the peninsula. The main span lies in rubble, blocking maritime traffic and the resupply of Russian troops fighting Ukraine. 

But standing with Xi and Trump, Putin will look like one of the three main leaders of the world, not the instigator of a war which has cost Russia almost half a million military dead, according to reports – with no end in sight.

The stakes

President Trump is a supplicant at this meeting – to the point where it is dangerous for him to enter into negotiations. He wants to talk about curbing the growth or renewal of nuclear weapons arsenals, partly with a view to bringing down cost. But China has said from the beginning this is a non-starter, given that its nuclear arsenal is far behind those of the other two. 

Trump may also want to push China on critical minerals: he has accused Beijing of not making good on the deal struck a year ago in South Korea. But as then, when he threatened tariffs only to swiftly back down when Xi threatened to withhold minerals supplies, he will find he has a weak hand.

He will be similarly on the back foot if Xi presses him to ensure the continued supply of top US chips from Nvidia, whether legally exported or through intermediaries. The defenestration of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO over a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy complicates the picture. But the fact remains, despite the weight of opinion in Congress and the opposition of Trump’s top team, Trump, Huang and commerce secretary Howard Lutnick have facilitated the chip trade with China. Should Trump try to change direction, it would not be surprising if Xi threatened to turn off minerals supply once again. 

The wars in Ukraine and Iran are not likely to get useful attention from the trio. China has no incentive to get involved in Iran, a war of Trump’s making from which he is trying to extricate the US. And Beijing is quietly stirring the conflict in Ukraine, helping Russia by buying its oil and selling it engines and components used in aerial warfare. Having Europe preoccupied with the conflict suits China fine. 

The danger for Ukraine is that Trump uses this summit to try to advance his notion of peace, including giving Russia territory it has not managed to seize by force. It is striking that Ukraine made a point of saying that its strike on Kerch bridge was conducted without Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite communication system, which it accuses the US of turning off or switching to slower speeds to put pressure on Kyiv. 

Ukraine will be able to hold out, but only with European help. There is bitterness among Ukrainian officials that despite the heavy rebuff to Trump in the US mid-term elections, a Democrat-dominated Congress – while talking tougher on Putin – is unlikely to send more funds Ukraine’s way. 

Become a corporate member

Europe, not present at this summit, is in the crosshairs of all three leaders. Trump remains in open dispute with European leaders over their dependency on US defence and alleged cultural decline. China is unhappy about the tariffs the EU is now considering, targeting its exports. And Russia is of course probing European unity over Ukraine. 

European leaders, including the UK, need to look hard at this trio and work out their response on security and trade. They have every incentive to work out a common front: a live war is taking place on their eastern flank, as their main security guarantor becomes increasingly unpredictable. And technological competition from China threatens to annihilate their manufacturing industries. 

Other countries will look at the same photograph and similarly count their friends and new alliances. The smaller the country, the more it needs the rule of international law and respect for international institutions. 

Xi, Trump and Putin may gather believing they dominate the world. But their meeting gives others every reason to look for ways to stand together.
