title: Shifting Landscapes: The Impact of Agricultural Innovation on Deforestation
author: Décamps, Marie Louise
description: This paper examines the direct and indirect effects of agricultural technological change on deforestation using the introduction of genetically modified soy in the Brazilian Amazon. Soy production replaced more land and labor-intensive cattle ranching, slowing local deforestation. However, displaced cattle ranching relocated to connected areas, clearing forest elsewhere and offsetting 39 percent of the forest that was spared locally. Displacement is mediated by the road network, which enables labor mobility and continued access to fixed slaughterhouses. On net, the introduction of genetically modified soy preserved approximately 25,600 square kilometers of forest between 2003 and 2010.

title: Digital Land Rights and Rural Credit Access: Lessons from Village Habitation (Abadi) Land Titling in India
author: Deininger, Klaus W.
description: To test whether the overwhelming finding of zero credit effects from rural land titling in the literature can be attributed to a perception of registries as static document stores and a narrow focus on agricultural land, this paper explores India’s Survey of Villages Abadi and Mapping with Improvised Technology in Village Areas program. This program issued property cards at low cost to rural residential homesteads, the only asset for the 56 percent of rural households owning no agricultural land, in a way that is digitally integrated into national lending infrastructure. Heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences estimates across 42,000 villages in Madhya Pradesh show that property card issuance created sustained land and credit market activity from zero and reached remote communities as effectively as those near bank branches. This reframes an ideologically charged debate into an actionable agenda that views property registries as key digital public infrastructure, one that India’s ongoing digitization and regulatory reforms are well-placed to advance.

title: The Philippines did not deliver a South China Sea Code of Conduct. But it has shown what ASEAN can achieve
author: jon.wallace
description:
The Philippines did not deliver a South China Sea Code of Conduct. But it has shown what ASEAN can achieve Expert comment jon.wallace 17 November 2026

This week’s summit did not produce the Code many desire. But as ASEAN Chair Manila has laid a useful foundation for the Code, while making important progress on regional connectivity.

When it assumed the Chair of ASEAN last year, the Philippines placed negotiations to establish a South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) at the centre of its agenda. An agreement has been desired for decades, to help reduce territorial and other tensions between China and regional countries. The need for the COC is clear: Philippine ships have continued to clash with Chinese Coast Guard vessels throughout the year, around disputed areas such as Scarborough Shoal. 

But Philippines Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro cooled expectations of an agreement at this week’s ASEAN summit. In a recent statement, she said that while around 80 per cent of the provisions are agreed, ‘sticking points’ still remain. It is therefore unlikely to be concluded by the end of the year with Philippines as ASEAN Chair.

But the Philippines tenure has been about more than just the COC. In a region of diverging priorities, security alignments, and threat perceptions, Manila should be judged by how far it has boosted ASEAN’s utility as an independent diplomatic actor able to strengthen regional solidarity.

Progress under pressure

The role of ASEAN Chair was clearly going to test the Philippines: How would it reconcile its national security interests with its responsibilities as the leader of a forum for regional cooperation? And would Beijing see Manila as a good faith actor on the COC?

The Philippines is, after all, one of the oldest treaty partners of the US. Those ties are getting stronger under President Ferdinand ‘Bongbong’ Marcos, while its relationship with China becomes ever more fractious – a stance not shared by all ASEAN partners. 

Beside these obvious impediments, the overlapping and complex nature of the claims in South China Sea waters made the COC a tricky subject to negotiate within the bloc, let alone with China. But under the stewardship of the Philippines delegations met every month this year and have managed to produce a substantial part of an agreement – a significant jump after two decades of diplomatic deadlock. 

There is no official confirmation on what the sticking points were, but past statements suggest issues around legal implementation, geographical scope, and terms of reference prevented a final agreement. Singapore, next year’s chair, enjoys a more stable relationship with Beijing and may stand a better chance of ironing out these final elements. Even this remains uncertain, but setting up Singapore with the best possible chance always looked like the most realistic ambition for the Philippines on the COC, and it has made good progress to that end. 

Outside of COC negotiations, the Philippines has managed to make significant moves on some other stated priorities. The Philippines assumed the Chair of ASEAN under the theme ‘Navigating our future, together’. This focussed on three core pillars: Peace and security anchors, prosperity corridors, and people empowerment. 

To this end, Manila concluded negotiations of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA). This is the world’s first binding region-wide digital economy deal, which will better integrate the region and foster greater cross-border data flows and end-to-end digital trade, promising to bring in $2 trillion by 2030. 

The Philippines also championed the ASEAN Leaders’ Declaration on Strategic Trade Management, which aims to establish unified frameworks to strengthen the resilience of regional supply chains. 

And it established the ASEAN Centre of Excellence for Creative Industries, fostering a more interconnected creative economy and greater cultural exchange. Manila has also pushed for greater collaboration on disaster preparedness, with a focus on pooling resources in the face of natural calamities.

One significant area where little has been achieved is the crisis in Myanmar: diplomatic progress on the issue was a strategic and symbolic challenge for the Philippines and ASEAN’s credibility as a peace-making body. In the end, ASEAN’s agenda remains stalled. The summit agreed to pursue ‘calibrated engagement’ in pursuit of ASEAN’s ‘5 Point Consensus’, and leaves the door open for gradual restoration to the bloc. But as a unified group, ASEAN appears to have little hope of influencing Myanmar’s military government.

Successful summitry 

This summit needed to go well for President Marcos. The Philippines has been pursuing its ASEAN agenda at a time of mounting domestic pressure. The war in Iran has strained energy supply chains, hindering access to necessities. Summer saw massive losses from tsunamis and earthquakes, and impeachment proceedings against the Vice President. The Marcos administration received its lowest ever approval ratings this month, as protestors clashed with police on the eve of the summit. 

Want to hear more on the future of global trade?

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

The event was ostensibly been productive. More than 150 outcome documents were reviewed and approved. A new ASEAN free trade agreement has been agreed with Canada. Brazil and Canada have committed $540 million for rainforest protection. And the event presented a significant opportunity for the bloc to interact with influential leaders including President Donald Trump, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Prime Minister Mark Carney, and President Lula da Silva.

And as always at summits, meetings on the sidelines provided opportunities for important diplomacy: Japan’s PM Takaichi and South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung held their fourth bilateral meeting. And the Quad convened for the first time in two years. 

But ASEAN countries must see real returns from these convenings to be considered a success. And it is imperative that ASEAN as a unit is seen as a key player rather than a platform through which bilateral deals can be done. Indeed, Philippines President Marcos emphasized a ‘whole-of-ASEAN approach’ in his plenary speech.

This focus on unifying regional interests is not for the sake of ASEAN alone, but part of a wider strategy to protect the Philippines in the face of broader geopolitical trends. The test will be if Manila can carry this sentiment forward beyond its tenure as chair – something that may prove difficult.

Preparing for the storms ahead

2027 will see Singapore become ASEAN Chair with the organization set to be tested by deepening faultlines on AI alliances, critical mineral exploration, and supply chain and energy resilience. 

Divergences are already appearing among members on how best to approach these issues. Coming on top of existing territorial disputes, strained relations within the bloc seem likely. However, even if ASEAN countries have diverging interests, they will never be able to escape the reality of what they share: geography and history. 

As the overlapping threats of climate change, great power rivalry, and an unstable global economy demand a cohesive regional response, the Philippines’ priorities of cohesion and greater interdependence will be key to the region’s survival. What this year has made clear is that grand international dealmaking of the kind represented by the COC may continue to prove difficult for the group. Despite this, ASEAN can provide an indispensable function, facilitating interoperability and integration that fuels growth and secures sovereignty. 

As President Marcos said at the summit’s opening, the coming years will be about ‘not only where ASEAN is headed, but what ASEAN must become’. For years the ASEAN has been dismissed as ineffectual and underperforming. But the group has endured. And the Philippines period as Chair has perhaps shown the bloc’s true value – driving incremental but unyielding change towards an increasingly interconnected region.

description: Bulgaria has made remarkable progress in recent years, becoming a high-income country in 2024 and joining the eurozone in 2026. Yet important structural challenges remain. This Country Climate and Development Report (CCDR) examines how Bulgaria can continue converging with the European Union while transitioning to a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy. At the same time, the report recognizes that the transition must be managed carefully to ensure that its benefits are broadly shared. title: The UK and the EU need an economic security partnership
author: thilton.drupal
description:
The UK and the EU need an economic security partnership Expert comment thilton.drupal 16 November 2026

The UK–EU Summit is an opportunity to secure a new partnership suitable for an increasingly hostile global economy. It should start with an information-sharing arrangement about high-risk investments, including from China.

The second UK–EU ‘reset’ summit takes place on 20 November, after a six-month delay to give prime minister Andy Burnham’s new government time to settle in and set its priorities. 

It is expected to deliver on the deals kickstarted by the Starmer government, most of which focus on reducing barriers to trade and mobility. These include a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement that removes most checks on trade in animals, plants, and their products, as well as a youth experience scheme and the linking of the UK and EU emissions trading systems. Completing these agreements is important for growth – the UK government estimates the SPS deal could eventually be worth £5.1 billion a year – and for building trust with the EU after years of political setbacks.

But the Burnham government will likely also want a more strategic partnership with the EU on security, defence and geopolitics. Central to this should be the goal of economic security, which has become a key priority for governments around the world. Economic security revolves around protecting sensitive national assets from hostile interference or exploitation, withstanding coercion and supply shocks, and building the strategic capabilities needed to stay competitive.

Beyond ‘Made in Europe’

Much of the reporting on this topic has focused on whether UK firms will be covered by the EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ initiatives. These measures – the most significant of which are in the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act – favour European-made products in public procurement and subsidy schemes, with the aim of rebuilding the EU’s industrial base and reducing its strategic dependencies. The concern is that, unless UK-made goods are treated the same as European-made ones, these initiatives risk shutting UK firms out of European supply chains.

Related work

Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose 

For now, the decision over ‘Made in Europe’ appears to have been kicked into next year. But ‘Made in Europe’ is only one part of the picture, albeit a critical one. Since Brexit, the global economy has become far more adversarial. The US is more willing to use tariffs as bargaining chips, while China is restricting exports of critical inputs such as rare earths to advance its geopolitical goals. 

In a forthcoming paper, we argue that middle powers such as the UK need to work together to manage these pressures. Partners like Australia, Canada, Japan and South Korea will be critical. But the EU is the UK’s most consequential economic security partner, due to its proximity, integrated supply chains and shared security interests. The UK’s approach to the upcoming summit should therefore put economic security cooperation as a crucial pillar of the reset in UK–EU relations.

Economic security partnership

The UK and the EU share challenges ranging from coercion and Chinese overcapacity to an unpredictable US. They also have shared dependencies in critical minerals, energy and some advanced technologies. 

A new UK–EU economic security partnership would give both sides a regular, structured mechanism to share information and coordinate on these risks. 

This partnership could build on existing structures. These could include the Partnership Council set up in 2021 under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, the 2025 Security and Defence Partnership, and the annual UK–EU summits. The partnership would also involve designated channels being established across each government to coordinate information-sharing and policy objectives as part of its structure. 

As part of this partnership, the EU and the UK should initiate an annual ministerial dialogue on economic security, supported by official-level working groups. This would compare assessments of geo-economic risks, including from China, and discuss approaches to coercion, industrial policy and overcapacity. It should also consider ways to jointly engage other like-minded partners on trade norms and to address geo-economic shocks, such as the energy price crisis that followed the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

From the outset, the partnership should also include a commitment to consult on how to respond if either side faces retaliation for measures taken together. This could apply if the UK were to align with EU tariffs or investment conditions on Chinese goods or capital, for example as part of securing ‘Made in Europe’ treatment. In this scenario, the UK should act within an agreed process for managing any consequences. That would give both sides a framework within which to negotiate how to align their economic security.

Start with protective tools

Aligning tariffs and industrial policy is politically and economically challenging. This is partly because the UK and the EU compete in certain industrial sectors and for investment. It’s also because the UK sits outside the trading bloc and cannot currently benefit from the EU’s single market or the Anti-Coercion Instrument (nicknamed the ‘trade bazooka’), its new trade tool aimed at deterring and responding to economic coercion. 

Rather than initially seeking this alignment, the partnership should therefore instead begin by strengthening cooperation to address the risks posed by hostile actors acquiring or accessing sensitive assets. These include data, technology and intellectual property.

Related work

China and its trading partners are moving towards an economic peace. But it is a fragile one

At present, the UK and the EU share too little information on investment risks, research security and vulnerabilities in critical supply chains. Closer cooperation in these areas carries lower political and economic costs than aligning on tariffs. And it plays to the UK’s strengths. 

The UK’s National Security and Investment Act (NSIA) is one of the more developed screening regimes in Europe, while the EU only recently made it mandatory for all member states to screen investments for national security risks. A practical first step would be an information-sharing arrangement between the UK’s Investment Security Unit and EU member states’ screening authorities. This would also help address concerns on both sides about high-risk investments, including those from China. 

Over time, this would make it easier to share sensitive technology, capital and research. It would help build the trust needed for harder decisions on industrial policy and trade defence. 

A more ambitious agenda

Once that trust is established, the partnership should pursue a more ambitious agenda. First, this should build on the information-sharing set out above to establish a joint early warning arrangement for supply-chain disruption as soon as possible, modelled on the aims of the US-Japan-South Korea system, connecting the UK’s Supply Chain Centre with the EU’s monitoring of critical goods. 

Over the next two years, it should also include a channel for coordinating responses to coercion, including how the UK’s emerging anti-coercion framework could work alongside the EU’s Anti-Coercion Instrument. And it should foster strategic industrial collaboration over the long term, including pooling resources and talent. 

However, while political will is growing on both sides, cooperation on economic security still faces challenges. The EU is wary of extending subsidy and procurement benefits without commitments that ensure reciprocal access to UK schemes and alignment on tariffs and investment conditions towards China. For its part, the UK will resist overt rule-taking or limits on its freedom to set its own trade policy. 

The best way to begin addressing some of these challenges is to start with information-sharing, which asks less of either side than full alignment. It would start to answer EU concerns about Chinese investment and build the trust both sides need for harder decisions later. 

The effort is worth it. Despite Brexit, the UK’s long-term economic future ultimately remains closely tied to Europe’s. 

This is particularly true when it comes to shared economic security. A forward-looking UK–EU economic security partnership would help protect both economies from coercion and supply shocks, strengthening the industries that both will depend on while navigating an increasingly hostile global economy.

title: The 1.5°C target will be missed. Where does climate action go from here?
author: LToremark
description:
The 1.5°C target will be missed. Where does climate action go from here? Expert comment LToremark 16 November 2026

Breaching 1.5°C will see climate impacts continue to escalate. But adapting to a hotter world must not derail efforts to stop further warming.

Only a decade after governments signed the Paris Agreement, the treaty’s goal of limiting global heating at 1.5°C is already slipping away. Overshooting the 1.5°C target is ‘widely assessed as unavoidable’, according to the UN. Even the Paris Agreement’s broader aim of remaining well below 2°C looks to be in jeopardy: under current policies 2.7°C is expected by the end of the century.

The climate challenge balloons above 1.5°C. COP31 president Murat Kurum said in his opening remarks at this year’s conference that even a brief overshoot would cause ‘irreversible loss and damage’ and stressed that the extent and duration of any such overshoot must be minimized. 

Breaching the 1.5°C target also means climate impacts will continue to escalate, far beyond what has been seen in recent years. It will usher in a new era in which the consequences of climate change become systemic and global. Meeting this challenge – and minimizing the duration of an overshoot – will require more than redoubling efforts to tackle the causes of climate change.

The need for adaptation

This year has seen many extreme weather events, from heatwaves in Europe to catastrophic flooding in Nepal. In some cases, they have been beyond even what climate models have predicted. This rapid evolution of climate impacts is not just causing greater destruction but also brings with it several strategic challenges. Take insurance, for example. A group of senior whistleblowers recently warned that the insurance industry is increasingly struggling to insure assets – including homes – due to climate risk and raised concerns about the viability of its operating model. Overshoot will only escalate this complex and fast-moving situation.

Related work

Europe’s summer of fires: Burnham must centre climate adaptation in policies

Spiralling climate impacts have meant that the climate policy discourse is increasingly focusing on adaptation: the act of protecting populations against unavoidable climate impacts. Although previously viewed as an issue largely reserved for climate vulnerable nations – or even an unhelpful distraction from emissions reductions or a form of defeatism – the speed at which climate impacts have progressed has changed the tone and focused minds. 

Stark public warnings are now being issued. The EU’s climate chief recently declared that Europe must prepare for 3°C of warming by 2100, while the European Commission has developed a framework for managing risks at the scale of entire social and economic systems. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, meanwhile, has reiterated that the climate crisis and nature loss are a national security threat of the highest order. The UK government has also established a taskforce to explore options for resilience to these mounting threats and appointed the world’s first climate-security envoy. However, despite increased awareness, there is a growing gap between adaptation needs and the scale of investment. 

The risk of derailment

The growing focus on adaptation is not without risk. Increasing demand for protection against climate hazards can lead governments to adopt piecemeal, band-aid solutions to emerging threats. These may exacerbate the underlying causes of climate change or generate new vulnerabilities altogether. For example, in some cases, coastal flood defences have led to biodiversity loss, ecosystem degradation and have increased flooding risks in neighbouring coastal regions. 

An even greater danger might be that, as societies increasingly experience the impacts of climate change, demands for protection will divert vital resources and attention away from combatting its causes, derailing progress in this area. There are early warning signs of this dynamic in Europe. In the wake of the 2024 Valenica floods, a climate-driven disaster boosted climate-denying politicians. Following the UK’s hottest summer on record, Reform Party politicians have argued that the focus should be on greater adaptation to extreme heat at the expense of mitigation.

While the imminent breach of 1.5°C might challenge collective belief in society’s ability to mitigate future warming, mitigation will become more urgent than ever. Every fraction of a degree of further warming edges us closer to crossing environmental tipping points, which would critically destabilize societies. Focusing on adapting to climate risk at the expense of mitigating further warming risks perpetuating the conditions which create the need for adaptation in the first place.  Now is the time for accelerated, and complementary, efforts on both adaptation and mitigation.

Adaptation can enable mitigation 

Want to hear more on the path to a secure energy transition?

Join us at our climate and energy summit, where policymakers and industry leaders tackle the toughest questions on climate and energy security.

Doing this will require politicians to anticipate how climate politics could shift in tone quite quickly as we head above 1.5°C, moving from a focus on mitigating a future problem to a demand to handle deadly consequences today. Without preparation, the derailment dynamic could become a major problem. Preventing this requires several shifts.

Firstly, politicians must be frank about the reality above 1.5°C. Destabilizing climate impacts will now only accelerate. They will go from discrete and local extreme weather events that hit agricultural regions and cities, to systemic and global episodes that hit supply chains and unsettle financial stability. Statements such as Miliband’s are a good starting point. Without such candour, what comes next will be more surprising and therefore more open to a kneejerk, short-term and maladaptive reaction.

Secondly, as impacts increase in frequency and magnitude, it is right that governments should prioritize protecting people and closing adaptation investment gaps. But this must always come alongside tackling the root causes of climate change by accelerating mitigation – which requires clear and consistent public commitments from political leaders about the need to do both.

Thirdly – to help with the above point – investments in adaptation measures should meet three criteria. One, they should maximize protection against climate impacts today and in the future. This means they must be robust across the huge range of possible scenarios ahead. Two, adaptation investments should complement, not work against, mitigation efforts. Three, the public should have confidence in these investment’s ability to provide protection.

Technologies for managing temperature extremes provide a good example of how these criteria can be applied. Air conditioning (if not powered by renewables) meets the first and third criteria but not the second. In contrast, heat pumps – which often have a dual function that heats in the winter and cools in the summer – meet the first two criteria. But they fall short on the third, at least in Britain, where they are not seen as effective protective measures by the population at large. Shifting that perception could help ensure that rightful demands for adaptation to heat extremes can accelerate, not undermine, mitigation. 

Systematically identifying the options that best meet all three criteria has yet to be done. But it would help create a new merit order of options and identify what work is still to be done, like shifting the narrative on heat pumps. It would ensure that investments in adaptation measures meet the challenge posed by overshoot: protecting people – today, from the symptoms of climate change, and tomorrow, by tackling its causes.

An integrated approach to mitigation and adaptation is the key to navigating 1.5°C overshoot. Like sailors who failed to sail around a storm, societies now must change tack. They must protect populations against the literal and figurative storm of climate change, while staying focused on navigating to a calmer climate.

title: When the lights go out, how will Europeans access their money?
author: thilton.drupal
description:
When the lights go out, how will Europeans access their money? Expert comment thilton.drupal 16 November 2026

Recent outages and cyberattacks have exposed the vulnerability of digital payments. The EU and UK should use their upcoming summit to develop compatible offline digital currencies.

Across Europe, economies have become increasingly digital, bringing significant benefits to businesses and consumers. However, growing reliance on digital payment systems means that when these systems fail, people are unable to spend the money in their bank accounts.

Sometimes, this is because of technical failures. On 20 October 2026, due to an extended power outage that paralysed Google Cloud services, millions of UK residents were unable to make card payments, cash withdrawals or bank transfers.

In other cases, hostile actors have launched cyberattacks that paralyse European payment systems. Figures from September 2026 show a 61 per cent year-on-year increase in cyberattacks across Europe, many of which targeted financial services.

These risks have prompted the EU and the UK to issue fresh crisis preparedness strategies, such as the UK government’s ‘Be Ready’ campaign. A key aspect of these strategies is the advice to keep adequate cash at hand in case digital systems go down.

However, the use of cash has long been in decline: only 3 per cent of UK adults mainly use cash for their day-to-day spending. Consumers increasingly prefer the convenience of digital payments, while many businesses no longer accept cash. This raises questions about whether people will have sufficient cash available when digital payment systems fail.

This problem is compounded by the fact that ATMs also require electricity to dispense cash. As a result, during a prolonged power outage or cyberattack, millions of consumers could lose the ability to pay with their cards and phones or withdraw cash from their bank accounts. 

During the 2025 Iberian blackout that brought digital payments to a standstill, many consumers without cash could not purchase even the most basic of supplies. Tens of millions of people were affected across Spain and Portugal.

Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) that can function offline offer a solution to this problem. While both the EU and the UK have floated the idea, they must engage in much closer collaboration on their development.

Offline digital money 

Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) are digital versions of existing national currencies that are issued by central banks – essentially, digital cash.

Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, CBDCs’ value does not fluctuate independently of the national currency. And while stablecoins also aim to maintain a fixed value against existing currencies, they are typically issued by private companies rather than central banks. 

CBDCs also differ from money held in standard digital bank accounts, which commercial banks owe to their customers. Unlike these deposits, CBDC holdings would not be exposed to the risk of a commercial bank failing.

The European Central Bank (ECB) is currently developing its CBDC, the digital euro. Its aim is to preserve the role of public money in the digital economy and reduce the bloc’s dependence on non-European payment providers. Similarly, the Bank of England (BoE) is drawing up a blueprint for a potential digital pound.

A key feature of the plans for the digital euro and digital pound is the ability to make payments offline.

During an electricity outage, conventional digital payments can fail because payment terminals lose access to electricity, online transactions cannot be authorized, or the payment provider’s infrastructure stops working.

The goal of both the EU and the UK is to build CBDCs that avoid these pitfalls and reflect the operational resilience of cash, albeit in different ways.

Related work

Europe could win the battle for the future of digital money

On the EU side, consumers will be able to open a digital euro wallet, and preload funds there from their commercial bank accounts. During a power outage, say due to a cyberattack, they could make payments using their phone or a physical card through near-field communication (NFC) technology. Payments would be settled directly between the consumer’s device and the merchant’s payment terminal, without requiring internet connectivity.

The use of physical cards could prove particularly valuable during prolonged power outages, as they do not require charging, unlike smartphones. The ECB is also exploring the possibility of integrating digital euros into existing payment cards rather than requiring a dedicated digital euro card.

Meanwhile, the UK is currently prioritizing a slightly different design. Instead of settling the payment immediately, payment instructions would be recorded offline, but the actual transfer of funds would only take place once connectivity is restored. 

Offline payments are not yet crisis-proof

While efforts to develop offline CBDCs are important, several challenges remain. The EU and the UK should jointly address them.

The first issue relates to the risk of double spending – when the same units of money are used to make two or more separate payments. Normally, double spending is avoided through real-time, centralized verification of payment requests. 

However, during a power outage, payment terminals cannot send these requests to banks. While both the ECB and the BoE have explored technical solutions to tackle this risk, additional work is necessary before deployment.

Another challenge relates to operational readiness. It is unclear why European consumers would be incentivized to pre-emptively fund their offline CBDC wallets, especially if they consider a power outage to be improbable.

Furthermore, European merchants need to possess battery-powered payment terminals for offline CBDC payments. During the 2025 Iberian blackout, even battery-powered terminals became unusable as their batteries ran out.

Why the EU and UK need to work together

The EU and the UK should collaborate on offline CBDCs for several reasons.

The first is their complementary expertise. On the one hand, the EU is further ahead in the development of its CBDC, with the ECB aiming to be ready to potentially issue the digital euro in 2029. On the other, the BoE can contribute valuable insights from its experiments with different offline payment technologies, particularly regarding trade-offs between security, privacy and usability.

Second, the EU and the UK are exposed to several overlapping threats. Given that they rely on common technological infrastructure, their payment networks are highly vulnerable to shared power outages and, even worse, to coordinated digital destabilization efforts by hostile actors.

Finally, European collaboration on offline CBDCs is necessary because of economic interdependence. The EU accounts for approximately 45 per cent of UK trade. Almost 77 per cent of overseas trips by UK residents were to Europe. 

Failure to collaborate would mean that, during future outages, European cross-border trade and retail transactions might become critically impaired.

Three steps towards more resilient payments

The EU and the UK should use their forthcoming 20 November summit to advance closer alignment on offline CBDCs.

The first step should be to establish recurring, joint stress tests of payment resilience. 

The ECB and the BoE can simulate a shared 72-hour power outage, testing whether CBDCs can reliably support offline transactions. This will help European policymakers to better tackle the problem of double spending and other operational challenges before deploying CBDCs.

The EU and the UK should also strive to bring their technical standards closer together. This could include the development of a prototype NFC payment terminal capable of accepting offline payments in both digital euros and digital pounds. Tests could be conducted across the Irish border, where sterling and euro payments intersect.

Lastly, they should explore the expansion of offline CBDCs to cross-border transactions involving currency conversion.

During prolonged outages, businesses may need to make new payments to foreign suppliers for essential goods. The EU and UK could test whether payment providers holding both currencies could facilitate offline exchanges, allowing buyers to pay in digital pounds or euros while suppliers receive their preferred currency.

As hybrid threats to payment systems become ever more severe, the EU and the UK need to collaborate more closely on offline CBDC standards. Otherwise, they risk being woefully unprepared when the lights go out next – with devastating consequences for their supply chains and their citizens’ ability to purchase essential goods.

title: The Impact of Digitalization and Technological Development on Tax Administration, Compliance, and Complexity: An Exploratory Study
author: Evans, Chris
description: The rapid pace of digitalization and technological development has fundamentally transformed modern tax systems. Advances in information and communications technology, artificial intelligence, and data analytics are reshaping the ways in which tax administrations operate, taxpayers comply, and governments design tax policies. Against this background, the paper has three specific objectives: to review the development and implementation of tax digitalization, to examine the impact of tax digitalization on tax compliance, and to assess the impact of tax digitalization on tax complexity. As part of the first objective, the paper considers, as a case study, the World Bank’s recently launched B-READY project, which highlights the growing importance of digitalization in the operation of tax systems worldwide. The paper draws on recent developments in Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, World Bank Group, and International Monetary Fund policy reports and the academic literature. The paper offers a conceptual framework for understanding the paradox of how digital transformation simultaneously promotes efficiency and transparency and reduces operational and computational compliance burdens on the one hand, while generating new forms of administrative and regulatory complexity on the other. The paper concludes by outlining key policy implications and suggesting directions for future research on balancing technological innovation with tax simplicity and equity.

title: Beyond Safety Nets: Designing Economic Inclusion Programs for Sustainable Livelihoods and Jobs
author: Sumanthiran, Shilohni
description: Rising socioeconomic vulnerability and constrained fiscal space are pushing governments to find ways to help households move off social safety nets (SSNs) and into sustainable livelihoods and jobs. About 2 billion people in low- and middle-income countries are inadequately covered by social protection. Yet exit from regular safety nets is rare: in Zambia's social cash transfer, only 1.1 percent of the caseload had exited, and 99 percent of those exits were due to the recipient's death. Economic inclusion (EI) programs offer a promising transition pathway. They combine income support with multifaceted packages such as business capital, training, coaching, and financial inclusion. A meta-analysis of 40 randomized evaluations across 26 countries shows that these programs raise household consumption by 11 percent and income by 15 percent. Benefits are 4.3 times larger than costs under a 10-year projection. Around 35 percent of EI programs globally are already anchored in SSNs, and building on government delivery systems can sharply reduce unit costs. This paper provides guidance on the design and operational choices that support sustainable transitions out of EI programs and off SSNs. It shifts the focus from "graduation," often misread as a single, permanent exit, to "transition." This reflects how households move between forms of support as their circumstances change. The paper organizes program design around the "4Ts" framework. Together, these four dimensions help programs embed economic inclusion in broader government systems: (i) Targeting: deciding whom the program serves, through dynamic social registries and participant buy-in. (ii) Tailoring: adapting pathways to diverse contexts, baseline capacities, gender considerations, and climate vulnerabilities. (iii) Thresholds: setting time-based and outcome-based criteria for when participants are ready to exit safely. (iv) Transitions: managing exit through phased support, durable market and financial linkages, and shock-responsive social protection systems. The paper concludes with practical examples and operational recommendations for policymakers and practitioners.

title: China has the APEC stage. But Japan may have the momentum
author: jon.wallace
description:
China has the APEC stage. But Japan may have the momentum Expert comment jon.wallace 13 November 2026

Tokyo cannot compete with Beijing’s economic firepower. But it offers Indo-Pacific countries a diplomatic and economic partner that delivers tangible gains without demanding allegiance in return.

The Asian Century is upon us with China as its visionary leader. That will be the message Beijing will hope to drive home when it hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on 18 to 19 November.
    
The summit is billed as a forum to address ‘building an Asia-Pacific community to prosper together’. But it will take place as the world’s most populous region grapples with challenges of energy insecurity, supply chain disruption, AI governance, and technological upheaval – and as growing geopolitical tensions are causing the realignment of international partnerships. 
    
Beijing has not shied away from promoting itself as champion of the Global South. But for Indo-Pacific economies seeking a partner to build consensus and tackle the region’s most pressing challenges, the momentum may well be with Japan.

Low expectations

China’s history of lifting its people out of poverty at breathtaking speed has been nothing short of remarkable. Nevertheless, there is a trust deficit across the Indo-Pacific, where Beijing has established itself as the undisputed regional hegemon.

Its vision for growth, as outlined in in its latest Five-Year Plan, seeks to make China the global leader in advanced technology by 2030. But there are concerns among regional countries that this will mean Beijing further exploits its dominance and exacerbates global economic warfare.

Meanwhile expectations for gatherings such as APEC, and the ASEAN summit in the Philippines preceding it, are low. The possibility of a display of unity, let alone a collective action plan, seems remote, especially as China will continue to leverage its chokeholds on the global economy. Instead, more attention will be paid to meetings on the sidelines of the summits, including a likely trilateral between Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. 

Those talks are expected to focus on the Iran war and denuclearization. A breakthrough on the war would be greatly welcomed, given the economic pain caused by the resulting higher energy costs: Southeast and South Asian countries including Vietnam have been hard hit. But the underlying concern for regional countries will be that shifting relations between the US, China and Russia could further aggravate their existing challenges.

China will remain an indispensable relationship for all countries in the region. But it is Japan that may hold the key to a collaborative path to address the Indo-Pacific’s challenges – one that might allow the region to continue its upward economic trajectory.

An evolving strategy

There are three main reasons that Japan could play a key role as a driver of collaboration in the region. 
    
First, Tokyo’s Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) strategy has evolved to meet the new strategic reality. Originally FOIP championed a rules-based order, quickly becoming the foundation for the Indo-Pacific strategies of governments including the US and European Union. Its weakness, though, was the reluctance of South and Southeast Asian nations to embrace it. That, and the geopolitical reality of weakening commitment to a rules-based international order.      
    
Tokyo has responded by developing the strategy around a pragmatic, results-oriented approach. In her May 2026 speech before the Vietnam National University, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi again stressed the need for a rules-based economic order. But she also set out how Japan intends to update the FOIP to reflect the immediate, practical needs of Vietnam and other countries across the Indo-Pacific.

That includes initiatives to build economic infrastructure ‘for the age of AI’, such as underwater sea cables and satellite communications, creating a ‘FOIP digital corridor’. It also means enhancing energy security for the long term, as outlined by the $10 billion Partnership on Wide Energy and Resource Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia), which Tokyo is expanding as it collaborates with the World Bank to advance regional energy resilience.

And it means boosting regional cooperation on artificial intelligence through an ASEAN-Japan Co-Creation Initiative for AI.

A trusted partner

Second, Japan has emerged as one of the most trusted and politically stable countries in the Indo-Pacific. In the latest State of Southeast Asia survey, Japan is ranked the most trusted major power by respondents in the 10 ASEAN nations for the eighth consecutive year. Nearly 66 per cent of respondents regard Japan as a responsible stakeholder that would do the right thing for global peace and prosperity. That puts it in a position to operate as a regional consensus-builder that can bring forward a roadmap for regional growth.

Granted, Tokyo has no interest in becoming a ‘superpower of the middle powers’. But it continues to embrace taking on a greater role in an increasingly unstable region that is facing growing economic risks. And it has shown an ability to overcome significant tensions and focus on results, for instance through its improved relations with Seoul – where pragmatism has generally prevailed as both Japan and South Korea have sought to cooperate over economic concerns, the increasing unpredictability of US policy, and shared regional security threats like North Korea.

Third, Japan has been committed to ensuring continued US engagement in the Indo-Pacific, including on trade. There has been growing discontent in the region about the economic damage caused by US foreign policy decisions, from tariffs to the war with Iran. But Tokyo has been resolute in promoting frameworks that would encourage the US to regain its position as a trusted economic power once again. 
    
Granted, the likelihood of the US joining a multilateral trade framework such as the CPTPP is highly unlikely, even after a new Congress is sworn in under Democratic control. But the US remains the only country that has the advanced technology and financial capital to compete head-on with China. And Washington will remain a critical partner for economic security in the Indo-Pacific moving forward.

Japan cannot single-handedly reconcile the Indo-Pacific’s divergent interests, and there is domestic political debate about to what extent Japan should take on a leadership role, given its own fiscal constraints. It clearly cannot match China’s economic heft nor the technological and financial firepower of the US. Moreover, the trust that it enjoys in Southeast Asia does not necessarily translate into becoming a leader. Yet that may be to its advantage as the Indo-Pacific navigates the shifting global order and adopting to new geopolitical realities.

What Tokyo offers is a partner that delivers tangible results without demanding allegiance in return. Japan is positioning itself not as a regional leader, but as the convener the Indo-Pacific increasingly needs.

title: Border Carbon Adjustments Revisited
author: Böhringer, Christoph
description: To address concerns about competitiveness and carbon leakage, countries with ambitious climate policies are increasingly looking to combine unilateral carbon pricing with border carbon adjustments. These measures aim to create a level playing field between domestically regulated energy-intensive and trade-exposed industries and their competitors abroad by imposing charges on the (unpriced) carbon embodied in imports and (potentially) rebating carbon costs on exports. At the same time, they are seen as measures that may have protectionist motivation and shift the burden of climate policy onto poorer developing economies that bear less historical responsibility for climate change, have limited financial and technological capacity for decarbonization, and may depend on carbon-intensive exports. For an informed policy debate, understanding how border carbon adjustments alter the economic burden of unilateral emissions pricing across all countries is essential. However, quantitative impact estimates derived from ex-ante simulation analyses vary considerably in the applied economic literature due to divergent assumptions on key drivers whose relative importance is difficult to distinguish from the outset.  Based on controlled simulations with a large-scale computable general equilibrium model of global trade and carbon use, this paper provides a systematic sensitivity analysis of three fundamental dimensions that determine the impacts of border carbon adjustments: (i) policy design choices; (ii) the price responsiveness of supply and demand; and (iii) the input-output data characterizing initial heterogeneities of production, consumption, and trade patterns across countries.

title: Fiscal Multipliers of Government Health and Education Expenditures: Evidence from Electoral Budget Cycles
author: Francois, John Nana
description: This paper estimates the short-run effect of government health and education expenditures—often classified as merit goods—on output in developing countries. A novel instrument is constructed to identify the fiscal multiplier, exploiting two features of the budget process and electoral environment: (1) approved budget allocations are legislated before the fiscal year begins and, given the multi-year nature of health and education programs, reflect planning decisions taken well in advance of contemporaneous output shocks, and (2) constitutionally predetermined electoral timing generates political incentives for incumbents to increase and accelerate the execution of planned budgets in visible sectors like health and education ahead of elections. The instrument therefore interacts budget allocations with electoral cycle timing to isolate the predetermined, electorally driven component of merit goods spending. The estimated multiplier is around 2. Multipliers are larger in recessions, supporting health and education spending as effective countercyclical fiscal tools. Furthermore, multipliers are larger where shares of merit goods spending in output are low, which reflects stronger stimulative effects where unmet needs are greatest. Additionally, better institutions, proxied by control of corruption, condition the size of the multiplier. These findings suggest that health and education spending can yield a dual dividend, boosting economic activity even before their well-known longer-term productivity gains of a healthier, more educated population materialize.

title: Shifting Sands: Is Trade Still a Path to Development?
author: Barattieri, Alessandro
description:
The 21st century risks becoming an era of trade skepticism. The export-led growth model that transformed East Asia is increasingly seen as out of reach for today’s developing countries.

Four powerful forces are shifting the sands beneath them. Developing countries are caught between the Scylla of US trade protectionism and the Charybdis of China’s manufacturing dominance. New technologies are raising productivity while weakening the link between growth and jobs. Climate change—and policies to combat it—threaten to redraw patterns of comparative advantage. And demographic change is transforming where the world’s workers are and where competitive strengths will arise.

Shifting Sands: Is Trade Still a Path to Development? asks what these forces mean for trade, growth, and jobs, and it reaches a cautiously optimistic conclusion: Trade can still be a path to prosperity. The choices of major powers matter. However, an excessive focus on what China, the United States, and other large economies do risks obscuring a more important truth: Today, developing countries are the masters of their own fate.

In a world where competitiveness is critically linked to services and technology—and these, in turn, to skills and scale—developing countries must respond to foreign protection by implementing domestic reform, especially in transport, finance, and business services; to technological disruption, by embracing rather than resisting innovation; to skills shortages, by expanding both capabilities and opportunities; and to stalled multilateralism, by deepening international cooperation.

title: Europe faces faster cyberattacks than ever. But many of the solutions are long known
author: thilton.drupal
description:
Europe faces faster cyberattacks than ever. But many of the solutions are long known Expert comment thilton.drupal 10 November 2026

Cyberattacks against Europe are becoming more frequent and more damaging. Yet while AI has lowered the barrier to entry, most attacks still exploit old and familiar weaknesses.

Last month, hackers caused tons of food to be thrown away after hacking into refrigerators in around 700 French supermarkets. Within weeks, similar incidents were reported in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and elsewhere. Nobody has claimed responsibility, but France has accused Iran of carrying out the ‘unprecedented attack’ against it.

The freezer attacks come after a spate of cyber incidents across Europe in the last few years that have repeatedly exposed familiar weaknesses. Russia’s war against Ukraine has raised the stakes, putting Europe on the front line of hybrid attacks including through cyber operations. 

Four problems stand out: old systems that are never fixed, new technology built without security in mind, increasingly capable attackers aided by AI, and states using cyberattacks as instruments of power, often through proxies. 

Each requires its own response, and Europe is doing better on some fronts than on others. None is a European problem alone, and none will be solved by Europe alone.

Vulnerable legacy systems 

The first problem lies in the weakness already built into the technology Europe runs on. Much of Europe still relies on legacy systems – technology that has reached the end of its life and no longer receives the security patches it needs. The result is a stock of known vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit.

The freezer attacks show what this looks like in practice. They were not technically complex: most of the hacked temperature controllers in France were reportedly legacy systems that no longer receive updates. Operational technology of this kind, which controls physical equipment, often stays in service for decades, long after anyone is updating it. 

This is not just an issue for companies. The UK’s National Audit Office found in 2025 that government departments used ‘hundreds of ageing legacy IT systems.’ Germany’s federal audit office found in 2025 that parts of the federal government’s networks are so outdated they no longer receive security updates.

Part of the problem is visibility: organizations and governments often lack a clear picture of the technology they own and operate. Even when organizations know where the problems lie, replacing old systems is expensive and disruptive. But leaving them in place is becoming increasingly risky.

Replacing these systems is primarily the responsibility of national governments and companies that operate them. But the EU is also pushing for it. In July, the European Central Bank told Europe’s largest banks to replace or update legacy systems as part of planning for AI-enabled threats. The financial sector, however, is far ahead of most other sectors, and replacement will require money, expertise and political commitment.

In the meantime, basic measures, often referred to as ‘cyber hygiene’, can go a long way. According to ENISA, the EU’s cybersecurity agency, two-thirds of the vulnerabilities attackers exploit already have a patch available. Where equipment no longer receives security updates, organizations need to restrict its exposure or replace it. 

Europe does not lack information or rules: ENISA maintains a European Vulnerability Database, national agencies issue regular alerts, and the NIS2 Directive makes managing these risks a legal obligation. What is missing is implementation: turning warnings into action, particularly in smaller organizations, and enforcing rules that many member states have been slow to adopt. 

Technology built without security

The second problem is that too much technology is still being built without security in mind. This is due to market incentives; manufacturers compete on price, features and speed to market, rather than prioritizing security. The costs of insecurity have mainly fallen on customers and society. 

The EU has sought to change this. From December 2027, under the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), connected products that do not meet basic security requirements will no longer be allowed on the EU market. Manufacturers will be responsible for their security throughout their lifecycle. 

However, the CRA has limits. Manufacturers are required to report actively exploited vulnerabilities, including those affecting products already on the market. But reporting a flaw does not fix it. 

And for products that manufacturers no longer support, there may be no fix. Someone else then has to act: the shop, hospital or council operating the equipment must know it is affected and have the skills and resources to patch, isolate or replace it. 

The underlying problem is poor-quality software. AI could help strengthen the security of software by identifying and fixing flaws faster than people can. But that depends on vendors using AI tools (with human oversight) before their products reach the market.

More attackers, moving faster

The use of AI by attackers is compounding these problems. AI is accelerating the process by which attackers are finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in insecure products and ageing systems. It is lowering the skills and resources needed to launch attacks and compressing the time defenders have to respond.

This year, frontier AI labs made a series of striking disclosures about their latest models’ cyber capabilities. These capabilities are real, particularly when it comes to exploiting vulnerabilities including in legacy systems. The labs were right to disclose them. But the disclosures also showcased their products, and the hype and catastrophizing that followed have not always helped clarify where priorities should lie. 

AI is not yet changing the nature of the game so much as its speed and scale. ENISA found that attackers in 2025 relied mainly on off-the-shelf AI tools to sharpen skills they already had. Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre found that among the incidents it handled, AI had not enabled ‘a novel class of attack’. 

Related work

Is AI really getting out of control?

Instead, the greater danger is that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery gives attackers more opportunities to strike before system owners can apply patches. In response, defenders must be able to act at the same speed. 

Governments have not yet managed to achieve this. The EU, for example, created the European Cybersecurity Alert System to analyse threat and incident data across member states using AI. However, EU auditors recently found that the system had stalled and was not yet working as intended.

A separate challenge is dependence on external providers. Many of the most capable defensive AI tools are developed in the US. Access can be restricted or withdrawn, as US export controls showed in June 2026. Governments need to establish structured ways of working with these companies on early warning, model testing and making defensive tools available to operators of critical infrastructure.

Cyber as a tool of state power

The fourth problem is that states are increasingly using cyber operations as a routine instrument of power, often through proxies. As argued in this Chatham House paper, the war in Ukraine has exposed an entire ecosystem of proxies. The overlap between these actors blurs responsibility and complicates attribution. 

Europe does not lack the tools to respond to state-backed cyber activity. It has mechanisms for public attribution, criminal investigations, sanctions and diplomatic pressure. But these measures have been slow and applied unevenly, which has reduced their collective impact. 

Related work

Holding state-sponsored hackers and other cyber proxies to account

The priority is therefore to use existing instruments more quickly and consistently. This requires coordinating responses across Europe and with international partners.

An EU-wide response is only as effective as the national systems underpinning it. Yet all but two member states missed the deadline to adopt the NIS2 Directive, which requires critical sectors to manage risks and report serious incidents. Member states need to improve information sharing, strengthen reporting and practise their responses to attacks. 

Internationally, states have already agreed not to attack critical infrastructure or knowingly allow their territory to be used for malicious cyber activity. The UN’s new Global Mechanism on ICT security is where Europe and its partners should push to make those commitments count.

Familiar threats, less time

The attacks of the recent weeks may look new, but they tell a familiar story: known weaknesses, insecure products, more capable attackers and slow, fragmented responses. What has changed is the timescale. 

Europe has already written many of the rules. Its member states now need to secure or replace existing technology, ensure that what comes next is secure by design, put AI to work for defenders, and rehearse a coherent response with partners. 

That means not only strengthening Europe’s ability to withstand and recover from attacks, but also its capacity to disrupt those responsible and impose costs that deter future operations.

description: The report examines Kenya’s recent economic performance, fiscal and external vulnerabilities, and the governance and structural constraints affecting private investment, productivity, job creation, and inclusive growth. Fiscal pressures persisted as the deficit widened, public debt and interest costs remained elevated, and growing reliance on domestic borrowing increased risks to fiscal sustainability and private sector credit. Kenya’s external position weakened amid higher imports and softer remittances, although foreign exchange reserves remained strong, while rising food and energy prices contributed to higher inflation. The report identifies governance challenges, particularly corruption, as a major constraint to economic transformation, affecting revenue collection, public spending efficiency, borrowing costs, infrastructure and logistics services, firm performance, investment, innovation, and the livelihoods of informal workers. title: Will the US and Iran return to war?
author: jon.wallace
description:
Will the US and Iran return to war?  Expert comment jon.wallace 9 November 2026

That is not only President Trump’s decision. Iran may also reignite the conflict, in an attempt to break the US blockade.

In recent weeks there has been considerable speculation that the US would carry out new attacks on Iran once the US midterm elections were concluded. But with the vote complete, Washington’s next move remains unclear. 

In a recent 60 minutes interview US President Donald Trump said he did not see ‘any reason’ to escalate the war. It is possible that the president chooses not to resume military operations against Iran and settles for continuing the current policy of economic strangulation. But even in that case, a return to armed conflict cannot be ruled out. Tehran is unlikely to absorb US pressure quietly while its economy further deteriorates. This is the irony of the US naval blockade of Iran. There’s evidence to suggest it has effectively hurt the regime’s finances. Iran loaded no oil onto tankers in September according to some analyses. 

But the blockade is unlikely to succeed in achieving the strategic objective of forcing the regime to make significant concessions at the bargaining table. Instead, it might push Tehran to lash out, which would take all parties back to square one in this conflict.

Stalemate

The blockade of Iranian oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz has evolved over the past few months. Washington launched the operation back in April; eased it after agreeing to the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Iran in June (which allowed for the reopening of the Strait); then reinstated it on 14 July as the deal unravelled.

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Iran wants the blockade lifted and its conditions met before it reopens and stops its attacks in the Strait. Washington wants concessions on Iran’s nuclear programme before resuming any talks on maritime security.

It’s a stalemate. But it may not last long. The deep distrust between the two sides will make Iran doubt that US concessions will be durable enough to bring it lasting economic relief. Some in the regime will believe it is better for Iran to fight on its own terms than collapse from within as the economy is throttled. 

It will not necessarily require a new US military strike on its territory for Iran to lash out at its neighbours. In 2019, Iran responded to Trump’s economic ‘maximum pressure’ tactics with a series of attacks. In May and June of that year, it struck tankers near Fujairah and in the Gulf of Oman and shot down a US surveillance drone. 

Then on 14 September, drones and missiles hit Saudi Aramco’s Abqaiq processing facility and the Khurais oil field. The Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen claimed responsibility, but the US and Saudi blamed Iran. The message from Tehran was clear: We will respond to extreme economic pressure by attacking Gulf energy infrastructure. 

Defending a founding narrative

There are two main reasons why Iran responded this way to economic pressure before – and why it may do so again. 

The first is ideological. Iran isn’t just defending its shipping lanes and oil exports in this war. It is protecting its founding narrative of sacrifice and endurance. This is what Washington still doesn’t seem to get.

Since its founding, the Islamic Republic has staked its reputation on not just resisting outside pressure but also defying it. Sanctions, isolation, and military threats won’t coerce or bring down the regime: that’s the message Tehran keeps telling its constituencies and adversaries. The war with Iraq of 1980 to 1988 provides the clearest illustration of the regime’s commitment to that principle. Iran fought the war almost on its own, against an adversary backed by the US and Gulf states, and it survived. A difficult year or two as a result of a blockade is hardly comparable to what the regime endured at that time. 

The second reason is practical: Iranian defiance, unlike during the Iraq war, is now aided by outsiders. The biggest source of support is China, through its purchasing of Iranian oil. No wonder US officials have reportedly urged Beijing to play a more constructive role in ending the conflict. They understand that without China, the regime’s staying power will drastically diminish.

Tehran also knows that the Gulf states want the blockade to end. The status quo is causing them tremendous economic pain. The Iranian leadership is betting that if it holds out long enough, those with the most to lose from this economic crisis – Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and Kuwait – will press Washington harder to find an exit. 

There are limits to Iranian resilience, of course. In 1988, after Operation Praying Mantis (a one-off US strike against Iranian naval resources ordered by President Ronald Reagan) and months of mounting losses, Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini accepted a ceasefire with Iraq. He famously likened it to drinking poison. Yet it showed that when its survival was at stake, Iran could concede (if not surrender).

But the blockade is not the same situation at all. In 1988, there was no way Iran could have won the war. Continuing would have probably led to military collapse. 

Today Iran believes it has the upper hand. Listen to statements by Iranian officials, and it is clear they believe they have already won this contest. That’s partly true. The Iranian regime will, most likely, survive this conflict and possibly avert a new major US attack, which it would define as victory. 

But it still has to address the blockade. If history is any guide, Iran will at some point resort to violence to try to force Washington to reconsider. That, in turn, is unlikely to succeed: the US has its pride, too, and its interests. US officials are convinced that the blockade is working, so giving it up won’t be easy. If anything, Washington is doubling down by giving US Central Command the green light to establish a new task force meant to ‘prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.’

There’s only one way out of this stalemate: phased diplomacy, which the two sides are apparently considering. The basic sequencing is clear: In the first phase, Washington would need to partially lift the blockade in exchange for Iran reopening the Strait and ceasing all attacks against shipping. In the second, nuclear talks could take place, including the gradual lifting of sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian funds.

The two sides are keen to end the conflict. But they appear equally determined to avoid any perceived humiliation and Israel remains an unpredictable factor. Even now, it is not clear that sense will prevail.

title: After Trump’s midterm defeat, Russia and China will encounter a cooler US
author: jon.wallace
description:
After Trump’s midterm defeat, Russia and China will encounter a cooler US  Expert comment jon.wallace 5 November 2026

They may seek to exploit the president’s weakness, as domestic opposition to war with Iran hardens.

The comprehensive rebuff that American voters have given to President Donald Trump and Republican candidates in the midterm elections is likely to produce a small but important constraint on how the US behaves abroad. But it will also change how other countries treat it – allies, trading partners and rivals alike. 

Even with the Democrats in control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, the president retains much power over foreign policy – but not all. Congress is now likely to challenge any sustained deployment of forces in the Gulf. And it will reassert its authority over trade and tariffs, even if it does not amend the latter. 

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

The most immediate change is likely to be on the conflict with Iran. Voters put the cost of living – ‘affordability’ – top of their concerns. Yet, as they went to the polls, gasoline prices at the pump hit a high. Rising costs are largely a result of the continued conflict in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which Americans know Trump initiated alongside Israel and has failed to end. Trump could now indeed ‘lash out’ as some have predicted with more strikes, in an attempt to secure concessions from Tehran. But there is no reason to believe that a military solution will fare any better than before. 

The Republican party has been among the biggest losers from the war. The race for the presidency in 2028 started the moment the midterm results became clear. And GOP candidates are likely to be vehemently against continuing the conflict. Pressure within the US for a resolution will rise even if Benjamin Netanyahu, now Israel’s caretaker prime minister after his own electoral setback, urges a new assault. 

Ukraine

The change in Congress will probably not mean more arms or money for Ukraine. There is deep, rare consensus among both Democrats and Republicans that Europe should now pay its way on its own defence – and that supporting Ukraine is part of that. Trump has won that longstanding argument, they feel, and they have no desire to undermine that victory. 

However, the new Congress does not share Trump’s apparent warmth towards Russian President Vladimir Putin. Traditional hostility or wariness towards Moscow prevails. 

Trump, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff might still dangle business deals before the Kremlin, hoping for peace in return. But they will be constrained by a tougher mood and even formal opposition in Congress. No wonder that Putin’s spokesperson said, as the results became clear, that he hoped peace-making efforts would continue.

China

The same congressional wariness may well extend to China. One of the biggest disruptions that Trump could cause in his remaining two years would be to try to strike a deal with Beijing that included explicit acknowledgement of Taiwan as the sovereign territory of China. Trump’s recent decision to pause a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, to avoid aggravating trade relations with China, could be interpreted by Beijing as support for its views. Congress has, again across the political divide, been much warier of China. It now seems that some tech companies are leaning that way too.

The fate of Trump’s tariffs is unclear. For the moment they will stay, although Congress has been challenging the president’s right to impose them without its consent, through the Supreme Court. 

Politicians of all stripes find tariffs attractive for the revenue they bring. But others will look at the disruption to trade they cause (US car manufacturing was until last year interwoven with Canada’s) and their impact on inflation. That last point is hotly debated among economists given that inflation did not rise as much as expected when the tariffs were first imposed. But politicians in search of securing a lower cost of living may look again at arguments for repealing the tariffs. 

A city on a hill?

Most of all, the elections may change how the world looks at America. They go some way to answering the big questions raised by Trump’s second presidency: Have Americans changed? Are his actions what they really want, given they have voted for him twice? And is US democracy robust and capable of securing peaceful changes of power? To that extent, some will find the results reassuring. 

For US allies in Europe, Japan and South Korea, they may feel more confident in asserting their interests and values – although they will still be nervous of losing US support. Trump’s sudden apparent removal of arms support to Israel in the days before the election shows how whimsical that can be. 

For the US’s enemies and rivals, this result will inject uncertainty into their calculations. But it will also give them reason to probe for weakness, even if that is just by exploiting the repeated changes in policy inherent in the democratic system. Both Russia and China will brace themselves for a cooling of relations. But they will also explore the implications of the US being unable to hold consistently to its key positions for more than a few years. 

Given Trump’s personality and desire for attention, nothing can rule out impetuous and dramatic action, for instance on Iran or Taiwan. But he has lost any aura of being a winner that he retained. Politicians seeking to run in two years’ time will begin to distance themselves from him and try to constrain him from actions that could tarnish their chances. They may hope that he restricts his attention to the memorials in his name he is so keen to create.
